name: 2 Chronicles
sourceNote: Written freshly, thought for thought, from the oldest Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic witnesses (the Masoretic Text with the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Samaritan Pentateuch). © 2026 Jose Santiago. All rights reserved.

verses.text: Solomon, David’s son, took firm control of his kingdom. Yahweh his God stayed with him and made him tremendously powerful.{a}
Solomon sent for all the Israelites. He called the commanders over thousands and hundreds, the judges, and every leader of Israel’s families.
Then Solomon led the whole crowd to the hilltop shrine at Gibeon. God’s meeting tent was there, the tent Moses, Yahweh’s servant, had built in the desert.{b}
God’s ark, though, was no longer there. David had carried it up from Kiriath-jearim to a tent he pitched for it in a spot prepared in Jerusalem.{c}

But the bronze altar was still at Gibeon, standing in front of Yahweh’s tent. Bezalel, Uri’s son and Hur’s grandson, had built it long before. That was where Solomon and the assembly came to seek the Lord.{d}
Solomon climbed up to the bronze altar in Yahweh’s presence by the meeting tent. On it he sacrificed a thousand burnt offerings.
That night God showed himself to Solomon. “Tell me what you want,” God said, “and I will give it to you.”
Solomon answered, “You were so faithful and kind to my father David. Now you have put me on his throne.
Yahweh God, please carry out what you promised my father David. You have given me a nation to rule with more people than there are specks of dust on the ground.
Grant me wisdom and knowledge, then, so I can lead these people well. Without that, how could anyone govern this huge nation of yours?”

God replied, “You did not ask to be rich or to own many things. You did not ask for fame, or for your enemies to die, or even to live a long time. That is not what was in your heart. Instead you asked for wisdom and understanding so you can rule my people, the people I made you king over.
Wisdom and understanding are yours, then, as a gift from me. Beyond that, I will make you rich and wealthy and honored. No king before you ever had so much, and no king after you will either.”
Then Solomon left the meeting tent at Gibeon’s hilltop shrine and went back to Jerusalem. There he ruled over Israel.{e}
Solomon gathered a great number of chariots and horsemen: 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen. Some he kept in the towns built for chariots, and some he kept near him in Jerusalem.{f}
Under King Solomon, silver and gold became as easy to find in Jerusalem as rocks. Cedar wood became as plentiful as the fig trees growing in the western foothills.{g}
Solomon got his horses from Egypt and from Kue. The king’s buyers paid for them in Kue.{h}
They paid about 15 pounds of silver for each chariot from Egypt and about 3 3/4 pounds for each horse. Then they sold them again to all the Hittite kings and the kings of Aram.{i}

notes.text: Verses 1-13 are much like 1 Kings 3:4-15. Solomon comes from shalom, “peace.” David means “loved one.”
Gibeon means “hill.” Chronicles explains that Solomon worshiped there because the meeting tent was there (1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29).
Kiriath-jearim means “town of forests.” See 1 Chronicles 13 and 15.
Bezalel means “in God’s shadow.” Uri means “my light.” The Hebrew can be read “he had placed it” or “it was there.” “Went there to worship” may also mean “went to seek Yahweh.”
The Hebrew says “to the hilltop shrine.” The Septuagint says “from,” which fits the story.
Verses 14-17 are much like 1 Kings 10:26-29. Compare 9:25-28.
The Hebrew says “the Shephelah,” meaning “lowland.” The fig trees were sycamore figs.
Kue was probably Cilicia, in what is now southern Turkey. Some think “Egypt” here should be “Muzri,” a land near Kue.
The Hebrew says “600” and “150,” probably shekels of silver. The Hittites were descendants of Heth. Aram here means the kingdoms of Syria.

verses.text: Solomon made up his mind to build a house to honor Yahweh’s name and a palace for himself.{a}
He signed up 70,000 men to haul loads and 80,000 men to cut stone in the hills. Over them all stood 3,600 foremen.{b}
A letter went from Solomon to Huram, who ruled Tyre. It said, “Treat me as kindly as you treated my father David. When he was building his home, you supplied him with cedar wood.{c}

Look, I am about to build a house to honor the name of Yahweh my God. I will give it to him as a holy place. There we will burn sweet incense to him and set out the holy bread at all times. We will sacrifice burnt offerings every morning and evening, on Sabbath days, at new moon celebrations, and at the feasts Yahweh our God has set. Israel is to do this forever.
The house I plan will be grand, since no god compares to our God in greatness.
Yet how could anyone build a home for him? The skies, even the highest skies, are too small to contain him! And who am I to build him a house? It can only be a place to burn incense to him.

So please send me a master craftsman, one who is skilled with gold and silver, bronze and iron, and with cloth dyed purple, red and blue. He must be able to carve designs. He will work alongside the skilled men here in Judah and Jerusalem, the ones my father David chose.{d}
Please also send me logs of cedar, cypress and algum wood from Lebanon. I know your men are experts at cutting trees there. My workers will join yours{e}
to prepare plenty of lumber for me, because the house I am building will be huge and amazing.

To pay your woodcutters, I will give them about 120,000 bushels of ground wheat and about 120,000 bushels of barley. I will also give them about 120,000 gallons of wine and about 120,000 gallons of olive oil.”{f}
Huram, king of Tyre, wrote back to Solomon. “Yahweh loves his people,” he said. “That is why he made you their king.”

Huram went on, “Praise Yahweh, the God of Israel, who created the sky and the earth! He has given King David a wise son, full of good sense and insight. That son will build Yahweh a temple and build himself a royal home.
Huram-abi is on his way to you now.{g} He is a gifted man with great skill.

He is the son of a woman from Dan’s tribe and a man of Tyre. He has learned to shape gold and silver, bronze and iron, as well as stone and timber. He is skilled with fine linen and with thread dyed purple, blue and red. He can carve any kind of design and make anything you ask. Let him work beside your skilled men and those who served my lord David, your father.{h}
Now, sir, please send us the wheat, barley, olive oil and wine you promised.
In return, we will cut down all the trees from Lebanon you need. We will tie the logs into rafts and float them along the coast to Joppa. From there you can take them up to Jerusalem.”{i}
Solomon took a count of every foreigner living in Israel, following the count his father David had made. There were 153,600 of them.{j}
He made 70,000 of them carry loads and 80,000 of them cut stone in the hills. He put 3,600 in charge to keep the people working.

notes.text: In Hebrew, 2:1 is 1:18, and verses 2-18 are 2:1-17. Verses 1-18 are much like 1 Kings 5:1-18.
1 Kings 5:16 says 3,300 men were in charge. Counting the chief officers in 8:10 and 1 Kings 9:23, both books come to 3,850 in all.
Huram is another form of Hiram. Tyre means “rock.”
Judah sounds like the Hebrew word for “praise” (Genesis 29:35).
Lebanon means “white,” from its snowy mountains. No one knows exactly what kind of wood algum was. 1 Kings 10:11 calls it almug.
The Hebrew says “20,000 cors” of wheat and of barley, and “20,000 baths” of wine and of oil. A cor was about 6 bushels, and a bath about 6 gallons.
Huram-abi means “Huram is my father” or “Huram, my master craftsman.” 1 Kings 7:13 calls him Hiram.
1 Kings 7:14 says his mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali. She may have come from Dan’s family but lived in Naphtali. Dan means “judge.”
Joppa, today called Jaffa, means “beautiful.”
Compare 1 Chronicles 22:2.

subheads.1: Getting Ready to Build the Temple

verses.text: Solomon started work on Yahweh’s house in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah. That was where Yahweh had appeared to his father David. It stood on the spot David had picked out, the threshing floor that once belonged to Ornan the Jebusite.{a}
Building began on the second day of the second month, April to May, in Solomon’s fourth year as king.{b}
Solomon laid the foundation for God’s house 90 feet long and 30 feet wide, using the old measure.{c}
Across the front ran a porch 30 feet wide, as wide as the building itself. It rose 180 feet high. Its inside walls were overlaid with pure gold.{d}
The walls of the big main room were lined with cypress boards and covered with fine gold. Palm trees and chains were carved on the walls.{e}
He decorated the house with lovely, valuable stones. All the gold came from a place called Parvaim.{f}
He covered all of the house with gold: the ceiling beams, the doorframes, the walls and the doors. On the walls he had winged creatures carved.
Then he built the Most Holy Place. It was 30 feet long, as wide as the temple, and also 30 feet wide. He covered the inside with about 22 1/2 tons of fine gold.{g}
Gold for the nails weighed about 1 1/4 pounds altogether. The upstairs rooms were also covered with gold.{h}
Inside the Most Holy Place, Solomon had two carved statues of winged creatures made, and workers covered them with gold.{i}
Their wings stretched 30 feet from tip to tip. Each wing was 7 1/2 feet long. One wing of the first creature touched one wall, and its other wing touched a wing of the second creature.{j}
In the same way, one wing of the second creature touched the opposite wall, and its other wing touched a wing of the first.
Spread out, the wings of the two creatures reached 30 feet across. They stood upright on their feet, facing the main room.{k}
He made the curtain out of fine linen and thread that was blue, purple and red. Winged creatures were woven into it.{l}
At the front of the temple he set up two pillars, each about 52 feet tall. On top of each was a capital 7 1/2 feet high.{m}
He made chains that looked like a necklace and draped them over the pillar tops. A hundred pomegranates were fastened onto the chains.{n}
He set the pillars up at the front of the temple, one on the south side and one on the north. The one to the south was called Jachin, and the one to the north was called Boaz.{o}

notes.text: Moriah may mean “Yahweh provides” or “seen by Yahweh.” The name is found only here and in Genesis 22:2, where Abraham went to offer Isaac. Ornan is named in 1 Chronicles 21:15. Verses 1-17 are much like 1 Kings 6-7.
The months were counted from the new year in spring. This month was called Ziv (1 Kings 6:1). The Septuagint does not have “on the second day.”
The Hebrew says “60 cubits long and 20 cubits wide by the old measure.” A cubit was about 18 inches. The old cubit was probably longer, about 20 1/2 inches. Compare 1 Kings 6:2.
The Hebrew says “20 cubits” wide and “120” high. Some old copies say the porch was 20 cubits high.
The main room is the Holy Place.
No one knows for sure where Parvaim was. It may have been in Arabia.
The Hebrew says “600 talents.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds. The room was 20 cubits each way.
The Hebrew says “50 shekels.”
The meaning of the Hebrew word for “carved” is not certain. The winged creatures were cherubim.
The Hebrew says “20 cubits” for all the wings and “5 cubits” for each wing. Compare 1 Kings 6:23-28.
Or “facing inward.”
1 Kings 6:31-32 tells about doors of olive wood here instead.
The Hebrew says “35 cubits” and “5 cubits.” 1 Kings 7:15 and Jeremiah 52:21 say each pillar was 18 cubits, about 27 feet. The 35 may be both pillars added together.
The Hebrew says “in the inner room.” Many think the Hebrew word should be read “like a necklace,” since the pillars stood outside.
Jachin means “he makes firm.” Boaz may mean “in him is strength.” The Hebrew says “right” and “left,” which mean south and north when facing east.

verses.text: Solomon had a bronze altar made, 30 feet on each side and half as tall, 15 feet.{a}
Then he had a huge round tank cast from metal, called the Sea. It measured 15 feet across from rim to rim and stood 7 1/2 feet tall. A cord 45 feet long would just wrap around it.{b}
Below its rim were two rows of bull shapes all the way around, ten for every 18 inches. They had been cast as one piece with the tank.{c}
The Sea rested on the backs of twelve bronze bulls. Three faced north, three west, three south and three east. Their back ends all pointed inward, and the tank sat on top of them.
Its sides were about 3 inches thick. The rim curved outward like the edge of a cup or a lily blossom. It held about 18,000 gallons of water.{d}

He also had ten smaller bowls made for washing, setting half of them to the south and half to the north. These were used to rinse the parts of the animals for the burnt offerings. The priests used the Sea to wash themselves.
He made ten gold lampstands, following the pattern that was given for them. He placed them in the main hall of the temple, five along each side.{e}
He made ten tables and set them in the main hall, five along each side. He also made 100 gold bowls for sprinkling.{f}
He built the priests’ courtyard and the large outer courtyard, with doors for the large one. He covered those doors with bronze.
They set the Sea toward the southeast, on the right side of the building.
Huram also made the pots, the shovels and the sprinkling bowls. In this way he finished all his work on God’s house for King Solomon.{g}
He made the two pillars and the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of them. He made the two sets of chain netting to cover those capitals.
He made 400 pomegranates for the two sets of netting. There were two rows of pomegranates on each net that covered the capitals.
He made the carts and the washbowls that sat on them.{h}
He made the Sea and the twelve bulls that held it up.
Huram-abi made the pots, shovels, meat forks and all the other tools for King Solomon. They were for Yahweh’s house, all of shining bronze.{i}
The king had them cast in the Jordan Valley, in molds made of clay soil, somewhere between the towns of Succoth and Zeredah.{j}
So many items were made that Solomon never bothered to weigh the bronze.
Solomon also made all the other furnishings for God’s house: the gold altar, the tables where the holy bread was set out,{k}
and the pure gold lampstands, each with its lamps. These were to be lit in front of the innermost room, as the law said.
He made the flower decorations, the lamps and the tongs, all of the finest gold.

He made the wick trimmers, the sprinkling bowls, the incense dishes and the fire pans, all of pure gold. At the entrance to the temple, the inner doors that led into the Most Holy Place and the doors into the main hall were also gold.{l}

notes.text: The Hebrew says “20 cubits long, 20 cubits wide and 10 cubits high.” A cubit was about 18 inches. Verses 2-5 are much like 1 Kings 7:23-26.
The Hebrew says “10 cubits,” “5 cubits” and “30 cubits.”
The Hebrew says “ten to a cubit.” 1 Kings 7:24 says “gourds” instead of “bulls.” The two Hebrew words look alike.
The Hebrew says “a handbreadth” and “3,000 baths.” 1 Kings 7:26 says 2,000 baths, about 12,000 gallons.
Compare Exodus 25:31-40 and 1 Kings 7:49.
Or “basins.”
Verses 11-22 are much like 1 Kings 7:40-50. Kings calls him Hiram.
Compare 1 Kings 7:43.
The Hebrew says “Huram his father.” See 2:13.
Succoth means “shelters.” 1 Kings 7:46 calls Zeredah “Zarethan.”
The Hebrew says “bread of the face.” See 1 Chronicles 9:32.
Or “the door hinges.” Compare 1 Kings 7:50.

verses.text: At last Solomon finished all the work on Yahweh’s house. He then carried in the gifts that David, his father, had dedicated: the silver, the gold and all the other objects. He placed them in the storerooms of God’s house.{a}

Then Solomon called Israel’s leaders together in Jerusalem. All the heads of the tribes and families came. They were going to carry the ark of Yahweh’s covenant up from the City of David, which is Zion.{b}
Every man in Israel came to the king for the festival in the seventh month, September to October.{c}
Once every leader of Israel had come, the Levites raised the ark onto their shoulders.{d}
They carried up the ark, the meeting tent, and all the holy objects inside the tent. The priests, who were Levites, carried them.{e}
King Solomon and all the Israelites gathered with him stood before the ark. They sacrificed sheep and cattle, more than anyone could ever count.

Then the priests carried the ark of Yahweh’s covenant to the spot prepared for it. They brought it deep inside the temple to the Most Holy Place and set it down beneath the outspread wings of the winged creatures.
Those wings stretched over the ark’s resting place like a roof, sheltering both the ark and its carrying poles.
Because the poles were so long, a person standing just in front of the inner room could see their tips. From farther out, no one could see them. They are still there today.{f}
The ark held nothing but the two stone tablets Moses had put there at Mount Horeb. That was where Yahweh made his covenant with the Israelites on their way out of Egypt.{g}
At that point the priests left the Holy Place. Every priest present had gone through the cleansing rites, no matter which group he served in.{h}

All the Levite singers were there: Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and relatives. Wearing robes of fine linen, they took their places on the east side of the altar with their cymbals, harps and lyres. With them stood 120 priests blowing trumpets.{i}

The trumpeters and singers joined together as if with one voice to praise and thank Yahweh. With trumpets, cymbals and other instruments, they lifted up their song to Yahweh: “He is good! His faithful love goes on forever!” Just then a cloud filled the temple, Yahweh’s house.{j}
The cloud kept the priests from standing there to serve. The shining glory of Yahweh had filled God’s house.

notes.text: Verses 1-14 are much like 1 Kings 7:51-8:11.
Zion may mean “fortress.”
The Hebrew says “the seventh month.” It was called Ethanim (1 Kings 8:2). The festival was the Festival of Shelters (compare 7:8-10).
1 Kings 8:3 says “the priests lifted the ark.” Compare 1 Chronicles 15:2.
The Septuagint and 1 Kings 8:4 say “the priests and the Levites.”
The Septuagint and 1 Kings 8:8 say “they are still there.”
Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai. It means “dry place.”
Verses 11-13 are not found in 1 Kings 8:10-11. Compare 1 Chronicles 24.
Asaph means “he gathers.” Heman means “faithful.” Jeduthun may mean “praising.” See 1 Chronicles 25.
These words are sung also in 7:3, 6 and 20:21. Compare 1 Chronicles 16:34 and Psalm 136.

subheads.2: The Ark Comes into the Temple

verses.text: Then Solomon said, “Yahweh told us he would live in a thick, dark cloud.{a}
But I have built you a splendid home, a lasting place for you to dwell in for all time.”{b}
Then the king swung around toward the whole gathering of Israel. As they stood there, he blessed them.
“Blessed be Yahweh, Israel’s God!” he said. “With his own mouth he made a promise to my father David, and with his own hands he has kept it. He said,
‘Ever since I led my people out of Egypt, I never picked a town in any of Israel’s tribes as the place to build a house for my name. Nor did I name any man as ruler of Israel, my people.{c}
But now I have picked Jerusalem as the place for my name, and David as the one to govern Israel for me.’
“It was my father David’s deep wish to put up a house that would honor the name of Yahweh, Israel’s God.
But Yahweh told him, ‘You wanted to build a house for my name. It was good that you wanted to do this.
But the temple will not be built by you. A son who comes from your own body will be the one to build it for my name.’
“Yahweh has done just what he said. I have taken my father David’s place on Israel’s throne, as Yahweh promised. And I have built the house to honor the name of Yahweh, Israel’s God.
I have put the ark there. Inside it is the covenant that Yahweh made with the people of Israel.”
Then, in front of all the Israelites gathered there, Solomon stood facing Yahweh’s altar and raised his hands.

He had built a bronze stand, square, 7 1/2 feet on each side and 4 1/2 feet tall, and set it in the center of the courtyard. Now he climbed onto it. Then, with all Israel watching, he knelt down and stretched his hands up toward heaven.{d}

He prayed: “Yahweh, God of Israel, no god in the skies above or on the earth below is like you. You keep your covenant. You show your faithful love to your servants who follow you with all their hearts.
You have kept your promise to your servant, my father David. You spoke it with your mouth, and today your hand has made it happen.

Yahweh, Israel’s God, now also make good your word to David my father, your servant. You told him, ‘If your sons are careful to live by my law as you have, there will always be one of your descendants sitting before me on Israel’s throne.’{e}
Yahweh, God of Israel, please make that promise to your servant David come true.
“Yet can God truly make his home with human beings here on earth? Even the sky, and all the heavens above the sky, are too small to hold you. This house I have built is far too small!{f}
Still, Yahweh my God, please listen to me, your servant, as I pray and ask for help. Hear my cry and my prayer to you.
Watch over this temple with open eyes, by day and by night. You said this is where your name would be. Listen whenever I, your servant, pray facing this place.
Listen when I, and your people Israel, pray toward this place and beg for your help. From your heavenly home, hear us, and having heard, forgive.
“Suppose someone is accused of wronging his neighbor and is made to take an oath. Suppose he comes and swears that oath before your altar here in this house.{g}
Then from heaven, hear and take action. Judge between your servants. Punish the guilty one as he deserves. Declare the innocent one not guilty, and reward him for doing right.
“Suppose your people Israel lose a battle to an enemy because they have sinned against you. Then suppose they come back to you, praise your name, and pray to you in this temple, begging for mercy.
Then, from up in heaven, hear them. Pardon Israel’s sin, and lead your people home again to the land you handed to them and to their forefathers.

“Suppose the sky is locked up and no rain falls because your people have sinned against you. Suppose that, because you have brought hardship on them, they pray facing this place, honor your name, and leave their sin behind.
Then hear them in heaven, and pardon the wrongs of Israel, your servants and your people. Show them the good way to live. Then send rain on your land, the land you gave your people to own.

“Suppose the land has no food, or a deadly sickness spreads. Suppose the crops are struck by scorching wind or mold, or by swarms of locusts and grasshoppers. Suppose an enemy surrounds one of their towns. Whatever trouble or disease comes,{h}
listen to every prayer and every plea, whether from one person or from all your people Israel. Each of them knows his own pain and sorrow. So when anyone lifts his hands in prayer toward this temple,
Then from heaven, where you live, hear and forgive. Give each person what his ways deserve, because you know his heart. You alone can see inside every human heart.
That way they will honor you with awe and walk in your ways all their lives, while they live in the country you gave to our forefathers.

“Suppose a foreigner who does not belong to your people Israel comes from a land far away. He comes because he has heard of your great name, your mighty hand and your powerful arm. Suppose this stranger turns toward this house and prays.

Then listen from heaven, your home, and do whatever the foreigner asks. Then every nation on earth will know your name. They will hold you in awe, as Israel, your people, does. And they will learn that this house I built carries your name.
“Suppose you send your people out to war against an enemy, whatever road they take. Suppose they pray to you while facing this chosen city and this house I have raised for your name.
Then from heaven, hear their prayers and their cries for help, and give them victory.
“Suppose they sin against you. After all, everyone sins. Suppose you become angry and let an enemy defeat them and carry them off as prisoners to a land far away or close by.
Then suppose they come to their senses in the land where they are prisoners. Suppose they turn back to you and beg you there, saying, ‘We have sinned. We are guilty. We have done evil.’

Suppose they come back to you with all their heart and soul in that land where they were taken. Suppose they pray facing their own land, the land you gave their ancestors, and facing your chosen city and the house I raised for your name.
Then from heaven, your home, hear their prayers and pleas. Stand up for them, and pardon the people who sinned against you.
“Now, my God, please keep your eyes open and your ears ready to hear the prayers people pray in this place.{i}

“Now rise, Yahweh God! Come to the place where you will rest, together with the ark of your strength. Yahweh God, dress your priests in salvation. Let your faithful people be glad because of your goodness.{j}
Yahweh God, do not turn away from the king you have anointed. Remember your faithful love for your servant David.”{k}

notes.text: Verses 1-39 are much like 1 Kings 8:12-50.
The Hebrew word here means “high home” or “royal house.”
1 Kings 8:16 does not have the words “And I never picked any man … picked Jerusalem as the place for my name.”
The Hebrew says “5 cubits long, 5 cubits wide and 3 cubits high.” This verse is not in 1 Kings 8.
1 Kings 8:25 says “to walk before me.” Chronicles puts weight on the law.
Or “the heavens and the heavens of heavens.” Compare 1 Kings 8:27.
The Hebrew says “and he puts an oath on him to make him swear.”
The Hebrew says “in the land of their gates.” It may mean “in any of their towns.”
Verses 40-42 are different from the end of Solomon’s prayer in 1 Kings 8:50-53. Verses 41-42 come from Psalm 132:8-10, 1.
The Hebrew word for “faithful people” is hasidim, meaning “those who are loyal” or “godly ones.”
Or “Remember the faithful deeds of your servant David.” Compare Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 132:1.

verses.text: As soon as Solomon’s prayer ended, fire fell from the sky and devoured the offerings laid on the altar. Yahweh’s glory filled the temple.{a}
The priests were unable to step inside Yahweh’s house, since his glory filled it completely.

All the Israelites watched the fire come down and saw Yahweh’s glory over the temple. They dropped to their knees on the stone pavement and bowed with their faces to the ground. They worshiped Yahweh and thanked him, singing, “He is good! His faithful love goes on forever!”
Then the king and all the people brought sacrifices to Yahweh.{b}
King Solomon’s sacrifice was huge: twenty-two thousand head of cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep. That was how the king and the nation dedicated God’s temple.

The priests stood ready in their places. The Levites stood with the instruments King David had made to praise Yahweh, singing, “His faithful love goes on forever!” David had used them to lead the praise. Across from the Levites, the priests blew trumpets, and all the people of Israel stood up.

Solomon declared the central area of the courtyard before Yahweh’s house to be holy ground. There he offered the burnt offerings and the fat from the peace offerings. His bronze altar could not hold so many burnt offerings, grain offerings and pieces of fat.
For a full week Solomon held the festival, joined by all Israel. A huge crowd came from every corner of the land, from Lebo-hamath in the north all the way to the stream on Egypt’s border.{c}
They closed with a solemn assembly on day eight. They had spent seven days dedicating the altar and seven more days keeping the festival.{d}

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, September to October, Solomon let the people go back to their homes. Their hearts overflowed with gladness because of all the good things Yahweh had done for David, for Solomon and for his people Israel.{e}
So Solomon completed Yahweh’s house and the royal palace. He succeeded in doing everything he had planned for Yahweh’s house and for his own palace.{f}
Then one night Yahweh appeared to Solomon. “Your prayer has reached me,” he said. “This place is my choice. It will be my house, where sacrifices will be offered to me.
There may be times when I lock up the sky so no rain falls, or tell locusts to devour the land, or send a deadly sickness among my people.{g} At such times,

if the people who carry my name bow low in humility and pray, if they search for my face and leave their wicked paths, then from heaven I will listen. I will pardon what they did wrong and bring healing to their land.
From this day on, my eyes will stay open and my ears will stay tuned to the prayers offered here.
I have chosen this house and made it holy so that my name will be here forever. My eyes will watch it and my heart will be with it always.
“As for you, if you live your life before me as your father David did, obeying all my commands and keeping my rules and laws,
then your royal throne will stand firm. That is what I promised your father David when I said, ‘One of your sons will always rule over Israel.’{h}
“But you people may turn away from me. You may leave behind the laws and orders I set before you and start bowing down to other gods and serving them.{i}

Then I will pull Israel up by the roots from the land I gave them. I will throw this temple away from me, even though I made it holy for my name. I will make it a joke and a thing to laugh at among all the nations.
This temple is so grand now. But then everyone who walks past it will be shocked. ‘What made Yahweh treat this land and this house so harshly?’ they will ask.{j}

And the answer will be, ‘These people abandoned Yahweh, the God their fathers worshiped, the one who led them out of Egypt’s land. They grabbed hold of other gods, bowed down to them and served them. That is why Yahweh brought all this trouble on them.’”

notes.text: 1 Kings 8:54 does not mention the fire. Compare 1 Chronicles 21:26 and Leviticus 9:24.
Verses 4-10 are much like 1 Kings 8:62-66.
Lebo-hamath means “the entrance to Hamath.” It marked the northern edge of the land. The stream on Egypt’s border, probably Wadi el-Arish, marked the southern edge.
The festival was the Festival of Shelters, which began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 23:34-36). The altar was dedicated the week before.
The seventh month was called Ethanim (1 Kings 8:2). 1 Kings 8:66 says he sent them home “on the eighth day.”
Verses 11-22 are much like 1 Kings 9:1-9.
Verses 13-15 are not found in 1 Kings 9.
1 Kings 9:5 says “a man on Israel’s throne.” Compare Micah 5:2.
In Hebrew, “you” in verses 19-20 is plural. God is speaking to Solomon and the people.
The Hebrew says “which was high.” Some think it should read “will become a pile of ruins” (compare 1 Kings 9:8).

verses.text: It took Solomon twenty years to build Yahweh’s house and his own palace.{a}
After that, he rebuilt the towns Huram had given him and moved Israelite families into them to live.{b}
Solomon marched against Hamath-zobah and captured it.{c}
He built up Tadmor in the desert, along with all the towns in Hamath where supplies were kept.{d}
Both Upper and Lower Beth-horon were turned into fortress towns, with walls, gates and heavy bars to lock them.{e}
He did the same with Baalath and with every town where he stored supplies or kept chariots and horses. He built whatever he wished in Jerusalem, in Lebanon and in every land he ruled.{f}
Some people were still left from the nations that had lived in the land before Israel: Amorites and Hittites, Hivites and Perizzites, and Jebusites too.{g}
Israel had never wiped out these families. So Solomon made their descendants work as forced laborers, and they still do today.
But Solomon did not make slaves of any Israelites. They served as his soldiers, his top officers, and the commanders of his chariots and chariot drivers.
King Solomon had 250 chief officials to oversee the people.{h}

Pharaoh’s daughter, Solomon’s wife, was moved out of David’s City and into a palace Solomon had built just for her. “No wife of mine may live in the house of David, Israel’s king,” he explained. “Wherever Yahweh’s ark has been, that place is holy.”{i}
Then Solomon sacrificed burnt offerings to Yahweh on the altar he had built for Yahweh facing the temple’s front porch.

He followed what Moses had commanded for each day. He brought offerings on Sabbath days, on the first day of each month, and three times a year at the great feasts: the Festival of Bread Without Yeast, the Festival of Weeks and the Festival of Shelters.{j}

He kept to the plan laid out by his father David. He put the groups of priests in charge of their duties. He gave the Levites their jobs of leading praise and helping the priests with each day’s work. He also placed the gatekeepers, group by group, at each gate. David, the man of God, had ordered all this.
The priests and Levites did everything the king commanded, down to the smallest detail, including the care of the treasure rooms.
Every task Solomon had planned was completed, from the day the foundation of Yahweh’s house was laid until the day it was finished. So the temple of Yahweh was completed.{k}
Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and Eloth, on the seacoast in the land of Edom.{l}
Huram’s men brought him ships and sailors who knew the sea well. Together with Solomon’s crews they voyaged to Ophir. They came back with about 17 tons of gold and gave it to King Solomon.{m}

notes.text: Verses 1-18 are much like 1 Kings 9:10-28.
1 Kings 9:10-14 says Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in Galilee. Perhaps Hiram later gave them back.
Hamath-zobah means Hamath in the area of Zobah. Kings does not tell of this battle.
Tadmor, meaning “palm tree,” was later called Palmyra. It was in the Syrian desert. 1 Kings 9:18 has Tamar.
Beth-horon means “house of the hollow.”
Baalath means “lady.” It was a town in Dan (Joshua 19:44).
Amorites may mean “westerners.” Perizzites means “village people.”
1 Kings 9:23 says 550. See the note on 2:2.
Pharaoh was the title of Egypt’s king. It means “great house.” 1 Kings 9:24 does not give this reason.
Compare Exodus 23:14-17 and Deuteronomy 16:16.
The Septuagint says “until Solomon finished Yahweh’s house.”
Ezion-geber may mean “backbone of a strong man.” Eloth, also called Elath, means “big trees.” Edom means “red.”
The Hebrew says “450 talents.” 1 Kings 9:28 says 420 talents. Ophir was a land famous for gold.

verses.text: News of how famous Solomon had become reached the queen of Sheba. So she traveled to Jerusalem to try him out with puzzling questions. She came with a long line of servants and camels loaded with spices, piles of gold and valuable jewels. When she met Solomon, she talked with him about everything she had been wondering about.{a}
Solomon had an answer for every question she asked. No puzzle was hidden so deep that he could not solve it for her.
With her own eyes the queen of Sheba took in Solomon’s wisdom. She looked at the palace he had built.

She saw the food served at his table and the way his officials were seated. She watched his servants at work in their fine uniforms. She saw the men who served his wine, dressed in their uniforms too, and the stairway he climbed to go up to Yahweh’s house. It left her breathless.{b}
She said to the king, “Back home I heard stories about what you have done and how wise you are. Everything was true!
I refused to believe those reports until I traveled here and saw for myself. Why, they didn’t tell me even half of how wise you are! You go far beyond the stories I was told.
What a blessing for your people! What a blessing for these officials, who stand by you every day and listen to your wisdom!{c}

Praise Yahweh your God! He was so pleased with you that he put you on his own throne to rule as king for Yahweh your God. Your God loves Israel and wants to keep them strong forever. That is why he made you their king, so you would do what is fair and right.”{d}
Then she presented the king with gold, about 4 1/2 tons, plus spices in enormous amounts and many valuable jewels. Never again were there spices like the ones the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.{e}
Huram’s men and Solomon’s men also brought gold from Ophir. They brought algum wood and precious stones as well.
Out of the algum timber the king built stairs for Yahweh’s house and for his palace. He also made harps and lyres from it for the musicians. Judah had never before seen instruments so fine.{f}

King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba whatever she wished for and asked him for. His gifts to her were worth more than the ones she had carried to him. After that, she set out with her attendants and returned to her homeland.{g}
Each year about 25 tons of gold flowed into Solomon’s treasury.{h}
That did not include the gold brought in by traders and merchants. All the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land brought him gold and silver too.{i}
King Solomon had 200 large shields made of hammered gold. Each one took about 15 pounds of gold.{j}
Three hundred smaller shields were also hammered out of gold, with about 7 1/2 pounds in each. These he hung in the hall called the Palace of the Lebanon Forest.{k}
The king also made a large throne decorated with ivory and covered it with pure gold.
Six steps rose to the throne, and fixed to it was a footstool of gold. Beside the seat, left and right, were places to rest the arms, and next to each stood a lion.{l}
Twelve more lions stood on the six steps, one at each end of every step. No other kingdom had anything like it.
Every drinking cup King Solomon owned was gold. In the Palace of the Lebanon Forest, every dish was pure gold too. In Solomon’s time, silver was not thought to be worth much at all.
The king had ships that sailed to Tarshish with Huram’s sailors. Once every three years they would return, carrying gold and silver, ivory, apes and peacocks.{m}
No king anywhere on earth matched King Solomon in wealth or in wisdom.
Kings from every land longed to meet him and listen to the wisdom God had placed in his heart.
Every year each of them came bringing gifts: silver and gold objects, clothing, weapons and spices, and horses and mules too.{n}
Solomon kept 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots, and 12,000 horsemen. Some he stationed in the chariot towns and some close to him in Jerusalem.{o}
Every king between the Euphrates and Philistine country, down to Egypt’s border, was under his rule.{p}
While he was king, silver was as common in Jerusalem as stones. Cedar was as plentiful as the fig trees in the western foothills.
Horses for Solomon were imported from Egypt and many other lands.

Everything else Solomon did, from start to finish, is written down in the records of Nathan the prophet. It is also in the words of Ahijah, the prophet from Shiloh, and in what Iddo the seer saw in visions concerning Jeroboam, Nebat’s son.{q}
For forty years Solomon reigned from Jerusalem as king of all Israel.
Then Solomon died and joined his ancestors. They buried him in the city of David, his father, and Rehoboam, his son, took the throne.{r}

notes.text: Verses 1-12 are much like 1 Kings 10:1-13. Sheba was probably in the southwest corner of Arabia, in what is now Yemen.
Or “the burnt offerings he sacrificed at Yahweh’s house.” The Hebrew word here can mean “his going up” or “his upper room.”
The Septuagint of 1 Kings 10:8 says “your wives.” The Hebrew words look alike.
1 Kings 10:9 says “on Israel’s throne.” Chronicles speaks of the throne as God’s own.
The Hebrew says “120 talents.”
The meaning of the Hebrew word for “steps” is not certain. It may mean “paths” or “railings.”
The Hebrew is hard to understand. It may mean “besides what she had brought to trade.”
Verses 13-28 are much like 1 Kings 10:14-29. The Hebrew says “666 talents.”
Arabia means “dry land” or “desert.”
The Hebrew says “600 of hammered gold,” probably shekels.
The Hebrew says “300 of gold,” probably shekels. The Palace of the Lebanon Forest got its name from its many cedar columns (1 Kings 7:2-5).
1 Kings 10:19 tells about a rounded top on the throne instead of a footstool.
1 Kings 10:22 speaks of “Tarshish ships,” which were probably large ships for long trips. Tarshish may have been in Spain. The Hebrew word for “peacocks” may mean “baboons.”
The Hebrew word for “weapons” may mean “sweet-smelling oil.”
1 Kings 4:26 says 40,000 stalls. Many think 4,000 is correct. Compare 1:14.
The Hebrew says “the River,” meaning the Euphrates.

Compare 1 Kings 11:41, which names “the book of Solomon’s acts.” Ahijah means “Yahweh’s brother.” Iddo may mean “on time.” Jeroboam may mean “the people grow many.” Chronicles does not tell about Solomon’s foreign wives or the revolts in 1 Kings 11.
Rehoboam means “the people grow larger.”

verses.text: Rehoboam traveled to Shechem, where all the Israelites had gathered to crown him king.{a}
Jeroboam, Nebat’s son, was living in Egypt at the time. He had run away there to escape from King Solomon. When he got word of what was happening, he came home from Egypt.{b}
The people sent for him, and he and the whole crowd of Israelites went to Rehoboam. They told him,
“Your father loaded us down with a hard burden. Make our work easier and lighten the heavy load he put on our backs. If you do, we will serve you.”
Rehoboam replied, “Give me three days. Then come back.” So the crowd went away.
The king turned for advice to the old men who had served at his father Solomon’s side while he lived. “What answer should I give these people?” he asked them.
They said, “Be good to these people. Please them and speak kindly to them. Then they will serve you all your life.”
But Rehoboam brushed aside what the older men told him. Instead he went to the young men he had grown up with, who now served him.
“What do you say?” he asked them. “How should we answer these people? They want me to make their load lighter than the one my father gave them.”
The young men he had grown up with told him, “Here is what to say to these people who want a lighter load. Tell them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist!{c}
Your load was heavy under my father? I will pile on more! He used whips to punish you, but I will use scorpions!’”{d}
Three days later, just as Rehoboam had instructed, Jeroboam and the whole nation returned to hear his answer.
The king spoke to them roughly. He turned his back on the wise counsel of the old men
and followed what the young men said. “My father made your load heavy,” he told them, “but I’ll make it heavier still. He lashed you with whips, but my lash will sting like a scorpion!”
So the king would not listen to the people. God made things turn out this way so that Yahweh’s promise would come true. He had spoken it through Ahijah of Shiloh to Jeroboam son of Nebat.{e}

Seeing that the king would not hear them, the Israelites shouted back at him, “What share do we have in David’s family? We have nothing to gain from Jesse’s son! Go home, Israel, every one of you! David’s family, from now on take care of yourselves!” Then the Israelites all went home.{f}
Only the Israelites living in Judah’s towns stayed under Rehoboam’s rule.

Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, the officer over the forced workers, to the Israelites. But the crowd stoned him to death. King Rehoboam rushed to climb into his chariot and got away to Jerusalem.{g}
From then until now, Israel has refused to be ruled by David’s family.

notes.text: Verses 1-19 are much like 1 Kings 12:1-19. Shechem means “shoulder” or “ridge.”
1 Kings 12:2 says “Jeroboam stayed in Egypt.” The Hebrew words for “came home” and “stayed” look alike. The story of Jeroboam’s escape is in 1 Kings 11:26-40.
The Hebrew says “than my father’s hips.”
Scorpions here may mean whips with sharp metal tips.
See 1 Kings 11:29-39.
Jesse may mean “Yahweh exists” or “gift.”
1 Kings 12:18 calls him Adoram, and 1 Kings 4:6 calls him Adoniram. Hadoram may mean “Hadad is lifted up.”

subheads.1: The Northern Tribes Turn Against Rehoboam

verses.text: Back in Jerusalem, Rehoboam called up the best fighting men from the families of Judah and Benjamin, 180,000 in all. He planned to go to war against Israel and win back his kingdom.{a}
But Yahweh gave a message to Shemaiah, the man of God.{b}
“Speak to Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, the king of Judah,” Yahweh said. “Speak as well to every Israelite who lives in the lands of Judah and Benjamin. Tell them,
‘Yahweh says: Do not march out to fight your own relatives. All of you, go home! I have made this happen.’” So they obeyed Yahweh’s message and gave up their plan to attack Jeroboam.
Rehoboam stayed in Jerusalem. He built up towns in Judah to defend the land.{c}
He strengthened Bethlehem, Etam and Tekoa,{d}
then Beth-zur, Soco and Adullam,{e}
then Gath, Mareshah and Ziph,{f}
then Adoraim, Lachish and Azekah,{g}
and finally Zorah, Aijalon and Hebron. These became walled fortress towns in Judah and Benjamin.{h}
He made their defenses strong and put army officers in charge of them. He filled their storerooms with grain, oil and wine.
He put shields and spears in every one of these towns and made them very strong. So Judah and Benjamin stayed under his control.
Priests and Levites from all over Israel came from their districts to side with Rehoboam.
The Levites even left their grasslands and their property and moved to Judah and Jerusalem. Jeroboam and his sons had rejected them and would not let them serve as Yahweh’s priests.
Jeroboam had set up priests of his own choosing for the hilltop shrines, to serve goat idols and the calf idols he had made.{i}

After the Levites came others from every tribe in Israel, people whose hearts were set on following Yahweh, Israel’s God. They traveled to Jerusalem to sacrifice to Yahweh, whom their fathers had worshiped.
They made the kingdom of Judah strong. For three years they kept Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, secure, because for three years they walked in the path David and Solomon had walked.
Rehoboam’s wife Mahalath was the daughter of Jerimoth, David’s son. Her mother was Abihail, the daughter of Eliab, Jesse’s son.{j}
Mahalath had three sons with him: Jeush, Shemariah and Zaham.{k}
After Mahalath, Rehoboam married Maacah, Absalom’s daughter. Four children came from her: Abijah and Attai, Ziza and Shelomith.{l}
Of all Rehoboam’s wives and concubines, Maacah was the one he loved best. In all he had eighteen wives and sixty concubines. Twenty-eight sons were born to him, and sixty daughters.
Rehoboam made Maacah’s son Abijah the leader over his brothers, because he planned to make him the next king.
Rehoboam acted wisely. He sent some of his sons out to every walled town in the lands of Judah and Benjamin. He gave them plenty of supplies and found many wives for them.{m}

notes.text: Verses 1-4 are much like 1 Kings 12:21-24. Benjamin means “son of the right hand.”
Shemaiah means “Yahweh has heard.”
Verses 5-23 are not found in Kings.
Bethlehem means “house of bread.” Tekoa may mean “trumpet blast.”
Beth-zur means “house of rock.” Adullam may mean “hiding place.”
Gath means “winepress.” Mareshah means “hilltop.”
Adoraim may mean “two hills.” Azekah may mean “dug-up ground.”
Zorah may mean “hornet.” Aijalon means “place of deer.” Hebron means “partnership.”
The Hebrew word for “goat idols” means “hairy ones.” Compare Leviticus 17:7. On the calves, see 1 Kings 12:28-33.
Some Hebrew copies say “son of Jerimoth.” Mahalath may mean “lyre.” Abihail means “my father is strength.” Jerimoth is not named among David’s sons in 1 Chronicles 3.
Jeush means “he comes to help.” Shemariah means “Yahweh guards.”
“Daughter” may mean “granddaughter.” In 13:2 Abijah’s mother is called Micaiah, Uriel’s daughter. 1 Kings 15:1-2 calls Abijah “Abijam” and Absalom “Abishalom.” Abijah means “Yahweh is my father.”
The Hebrew says “and he asked for many wives.”

subheads.13: Priests and Levites Move to Judah

verses.text: Once Rehoboam’s kingdom was secure and he felt strong, he turned away from Yahweh’s law. All the people of Israel followed him in doing this.{a}
Because they had been unfaithful to Yahweh, Shishak, king of Egypt, attacked Jerusalem. This happened in the fifth year Rehoboam was king.{b}
Shishak brought 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. With him came more soldiers from Egypt than anyone could count. There were Libyans, Sukkites and Cushites.{c}
He captured the fortress towns of Judah and pushed on as far as Jerusalem.

The leaders of Judah had gathered in Jerusalem out of fear of Shishak. Then the prophet Shemaiah came to them and to Rehoboam with this message: “Yahweh says, ‘You walked away from me. Now I am leaving you in Shishak’s hands.’”
Then Israel’s leaders and the king humbled themselves. “Yahweh is right,” they said.

Yahweh saw that they had humbled themselves. So he gave Shemaiah another message: “Since they have humbled themselves, I will not wipe them out. Soon I will rescue them. Shishak will not be the tool that pours my fury on Jerusalem.{d}
Even so, he will make them his servants. They will find out how much harder it is to work for earthly kings than to work for me.”

Shishak, Egypt’s king, came against Jerusalem. He carried off the riches stored in Yahweh’s house and in the royal palace, stripping both clean. He even took the golden shields from Solomon’s time.{e}
To replace them, Rehoboam had shields made of bronze. These he handed over to the officers who guarded the palace door.{f}
Every time the king entered Yahweh’s house, out came the guards with the shields. When he was done, the shields went back to the guardroom.
Because Rehoboam humbled himself, Yahweh’s anger turned away from him, and he was not completely destroyed. Some good things were still found in Judah.{g}

King Rehoboam made his rule strong in Jerusalem and went on being king. He was 41 years old when he started to rule. For seventeen years he reigned from Jerusalem, the city Yahweh had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel as the place for his name. Rehoboam’s mother was Naamah, an Ammonite woman.{h}
Rehoboam did evil, because he did not set his heart on following Yahweh.

Everything Rehoboam did, from start to finish, is written down in the records of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer, in the family lists. Rehoboam and Jeroboam were at war with each other the whole time.{i}
Rehoboam then died and was laid to rest beside his ancestors in David’s City. Abijah, his son, followed him as king.

notes.text: Verses 1-16 tell more than 1 Kings 14:21-31.
Shishak (in Egyptian, Sheshonq I) started a new line of kings in Egypt. A carving he made in Egypt lists towns he captured in Judah and Israel, around 925 B.C.
Sukkites may be soldiers from Libya, or “people who live in tents.” Cush was the land along the upper Nile River, south of Egypt.
Or “some rescue.” The Hebrew says “like a little, rescue.”
1 Kings 14:26 adds “all the gold shields.”
The Hebrew says “the runners,” meaning the king’s guards.
Or “There were good things in Judah.” Compare 19:3.
Naamah means “pleasant.” Verses 13-14 are much like 1 Kings 14:21-22.
The Hebrew says “to be listed by family.” The meaning is not certain.

verses.text: Abijah became king of Judah in the eighteenth year that Jeroboam ruled Israel.{a}
For three years Jerusalem was his royal city. His mother, Micaiah, was Uriel’s daughter, a woman of Gibeah. Fighting went on between Abijah and Jeroboam.{b}
Abijah went into battle with 400,000 brave, hand-picked soldiers. Jeroboam lined up against him with 800,000 hand-picked, powerful fighters.{c}
Abijah climbed up on Mount Zemaraim in the hills of Ephraim and shouted, “Jeroboam and all you people of Israel, listen to me!{d}
Don’t you know that Yahweh, God of Israel, handed the throne of Israel to David and to his descendants for all time? He made a covenant with them that can never be broken, a covenant of salt.{e}
But Jeroboam son of Nebat, who was only a servant of Solomon, David’s son, rose up against his own master.
Worthless troublemakers gathered around him. They stood up against Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, when he was young and unsure of himself and too weak to resist them.{f}
Now you think you can stand against Yahweh’s kingdom, which he has placed in the hands of David’s sons. You have a huge army, and you have brought along the gold calves Jeroboam made to be your gods.

You chased out Yahweh’s priests, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites. You made your own priests, just as other nations do! Bring a young bull and seven rams, and any man at all can be made a priest of your so-called gods.{g}
But for us, Yahweh is our God. We have not left him. Aaron’s descendants serve Yahweh as our priests, with Levites at their side doing their tasks.

Every morning and every evening they burn offerings and sweet incense to Yahweh. They set out the holy bread on the pure gold table. As night falls, they keep the lamps of the golden lampstand burning. We keep the duties Yahweh our God gave us, but you have left him.

Look! God himself is with us, leading us. His priests are here with trumpets, ready to sound the call to battle against you. People of Israel, do not battle against Yahweh, whom your fathers served. You cannot win!”
But Jeroboam had sent some troops around to hide behind Judah’s army. So while his main army faced Judah, the hidden troops were behind them.
Judah’s soldiers looked around and found enemies before them and behind them. They cried out to Yahweh, and the priests blew their trumpets.
Then Judah’s army raised a mighty war cry. As they shouted, God struck down Jeroboam and all Israel in front of Abijah and the army of Judah.
Israel’s troops fled before Judah, and God gave them into Judah’s power.
Abijah and his troops dealt them a crushing defeat. Half a million of Israel’s finest fighters fell dead.{h}
That day Israel was humbled. The men of Judah won because they relied on Yahweh, the God of their ancestors.
Abijah chased Jeroboam and captured some of his towns. He took Bethel and Jeshanah and Ephron, along with the small villages that belonged to each.{i}
Jeroboam never got back his power while Abijah lived. Yahweh struck him, and he died.{j}
But Abijah’s power kept growing. Fourteen women became his wives, and they gave him twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
Iddo the prophet’s writings tell the rest of Abijah’s story, including his deeds and his words.{k}

notes.text: Verses 1-2 are much like 1 Kings 15:1-2, 6-7. Kings calls him Abijam and says he did wrong (15:3). Chronicles tells of his speech and victory.
Micaiah means “who is like Yahweh?” Uriel means “God is my light.” The Septuagint and 1 Kings 15:2 call her Maacah, as in 11:20.
These numbers, and the one in verse 17, are very large. The Hebrew word for “thousand” may sometimes mean an army unit.
Zemaraim may mean “two piles of wool.” Ephraim means “twice fruitful.”
Salt does not spoil, so a covenant of salt was one that would last forever. Compare Numbers 18:19.
The Hebrew says “young and tender of heart.”
The Hebrew says “to fill his hand,” a way of saying “to make someone a priest.”
See the note on verse 3.
Bethel means “house of God.” Jeshanah means “old.” Some Hebrew copies say Ephrain.
1 Kings 14:20 says Jeroboam ruled for twenty-two years. He lived longer than Abijah (1 Kings 15:9). “He died” here may look ahead to his death later.
The Hebrew word here, midrash, can mean “study” or “record.”

verses.text: Abijah died and joined his ancestors, and they laid him to rest in David’s City. His son Asa took the throne. Under Asa, the land enjoyed ten years without war.{a}
In the sight of Yahweh his God, Asa did what was good and upright.{b}
He tore down the altars to foreign gods and the hilltop shrines. He broke apart the stone pillars used in worship and chopped down the poles for the goddess Asherah.{c}
He ordered the people of Judah to turn to Yahweh, whom their forefathers had served, and to keep his law and commands.
In every town of Judah he got rid of the hilltop shrines and the incense altars. While he was king, the kingdom had peace.{d}
During those quiet years he built strong, walled towns in Judah. Nobody made war against him then, because Yahweh gave him peace.

Asa told the people of Judah, “Let’s build up these towns. Let’s put walls around them, with towers and gates that can be locked with bars. The land is still ours because we have looked to Yahweh our God. We sought him, and on every side he has kept our enemies quiet.” So the building went on, and the work prospered.

Asa’s troops from Judah numbered three hundred thousand, armed with spears and big body shields. Benjamin supplied two hundred eighty thousand more, archers with light shields. All of them were brave fighters.
Then Zerah, a Cushite, came to attack them. He led an army of a million soldiers, with three hundred chariots, and reached Mareshah.{e}
Asa marched out to meet him. In the Valley of Zephathah, close to Mareshah, the two forces lined up for war.{f}

Asa prayed aloud to Yahweh his God. “Yahweh,” he prayed, “only you can help the weak against the strong. Help us, Yahweh our God! We are counting on you. We have come out in your name to face this enormous army. Yahweh, you are our God. Don’t let any human being win against you!”
So Yahweh struck down the Cushites as Asa and Judah watched, and the Cushites fled.

Asa’s troops chased after them as far as Gerar. So many Cushites were killed that their army could not recover. Yahweh and his army had shattered them. Judah’s men hauled away great heaps of plunder.{g}
They attacked all the towns around Gerar, because Yahweh had filled the people there with terror. Judah’s soldiers took everything of value from those towns, and there was a great deal to take.
They also raided the camps where herders lived and took large numbers of sheep, goats and camels. After that they returned home to Jerusalem.

notes.text: In Hebrew, 14:1 is 13:23, and verses 2-15 are 14:1-14. Asa may mean “healer.” Verses 1-3 are much like 1 Kings 15:8-11.
The Hebrew says “in the eyes of Yahweh his God.”
The Hebrew word is Asherim. These were wooden poles or trees set up to honor Asherah, a goddess.

The Hebrew word for “incense altars” may also mean “sun images.” 1 Kings 15:14 and 2 Chronicles 15:17 say the hilltop shrines were not removed. Perhaps some shrines were used for idols and others for Yahweh.
Zerah means “rising.” The Hebrew says “a thousand thousands.” See the note on 13:3.
Zephathah means “watchtower.” The Septuagint says “in the valley north of Mareshah.”
Gerar means “place to stay.” Or “so that none were left alive.”

verses.text: God’s Spirit came over Azariah, Oded’s son.{a}

He went out to meet Asa. “Asa, and all you people of Judah and Benjamin, pay attention to me!” he said. “As long as you stay with Yahweh, he will stay with you. Go looking for him, and he will let you find him. Walk away from him, and he will walk away from you.
For many years Israel lived without the true God. They had no priest to teach them, and they had no law.{b}
Yet whenever hard times pressed on them, they came back to Israel’s God, Yahweh. They sought him out, and he showed himself to them.
In those days no one was safe going out or coming in. People in every land were in great turmoil.
One nation crushed another, and one town crushed another, because God troubled them with all kinds of hardship.
But as for you, be strong! Don’t let your hands go limp, because your work will be rewarded.”

Asa heard this message from the prophet, Oded’s son. It gave him courage. He swept away the hateful idols throughout Judah’s and Benjamin’s territory, and from the Ephraim hill towns he had conquered. He repaired Yahweh’s altar that stood in front of the porch of Yahweh’s house.{c}

Next he summoned everyone in Judah and Benjamin, as well as the newcomers living with them who had moved there from Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon. Crowds of them had deserted Israel to join Asa, when they saw that Yahweh his God was with him.{d}
This assembly met in Jerusalem during the third month, May to June, in Asa’s fifteenth year as king.{e}
On that day they sacrificed to Yahweh 700 cattle and 7,000 sheep and goats, taken from the goods they had captured.
They made a solemn agreement to seek Yahweh, the God of their forefathers, with every bit of heart and soul they had.
Anyone who would not seek Yahweh, Israel’s God, was to die, they agreed. It would not matter if the person was young or old, man or woman.
With a loud voice they made their promise to Yahweh. They shouted and blew trumpets and rams’ horns.
Judah was filled with joy over this promise, because they had made it with all their hearts. They had looked for Yahweh eagerly, and he had let them find him. So Yahweh surrounded them with peace.

King Asa even took away the title of queen mother from Maacah, his grandmother, because she had made a disgusting pole for worshiping Asherah. Asa cut the pole down, smashed it to pieces, and burned it in the Kidron Valley.{f}
The hilltop shrines were not removed from Israel. Even so, Asa stayed faithful with his whole heart all his life.{g}
He brought into God’s house the silver and gold and other objects that he and his father had set apart for God.
There were no more wars until the thirty-fifth year Asa was king.{h}

notes.text: Azariah means “Yahweh has helped.” Oded may mean “one who restores.”
This may speak of the time of the judges. Compare Hosea 3:4.
The Hebrew says “the prophecy, Oded the prophet.” The words “Azariah, son of” may have been lost (compare verse 1).
Manasseh means “making forget.” Simeon means “hearing.”
The Festival of Weeks came in the third month. The Hebrew word for “promise” in verses 14-15 sounds like the word for “Weeks.”
Verses 16-18 are much like 1 Kings 15:13-15. The Hebrew says “his mother.” Maacah was his grandmother (1 Kings 15:2, 10). Kidron may mean “dark.”
Compare the note on 14:5.
1 Kings 16:8 puts the death of Baasha (16:1) in Asa’s twenty-sixth year. The years here and in 16:1 may be counted from when the kingdom split, or the numbers may have been copied wrong.

verses.text: In the thirty-sixth year Asa was king, Baasha, king of Israel, came to attack Judah. He began building Ramah into a fortress so that no one could travel in or out of Asa’s land.{a}
So Asa took silver and gold out of the treasure rooms of Yahweh’s house and the royal palace. He shipped it off to Damascus, where Ben-hadad ruled as Aram’s king, along with a note:{b}
“Our fathers had a pact. Let us have one too. Take this silver and gold as my gift. Then tear up your pact with Baasha, Israel’s king, and he will have to pull back from my land.”

Ben-hadad accepted King Asa’s offer. He sent the leaders of his army to attack Israel’s towns. They conquered Ijon, Dan and Abel-maim, along with all the towns in Naphtali where supplies were stored.{c}
Baasha heard about it and gave up building Ramah. He stopped all his work there.
Then King Asa brought together all the men of Judah. They hauled away the stones and timber Baasha had been using at Ramah. Asa used them to build up the towns of Geba and Mizpah.{d}

Around then, Hanani the seer paid a visit to Asa, Judah’s king. “You trusted the king of Aram instead of trusting Yahweh your God,” he said. “Because of that, you have lost your chance to defeat Aram’s army.{e}
Remember the Cushites and the Libyans? They had a massive army with many chariots and horsemen. But you trusted Yahweh, and he handed them over to you.

Yahweh’s eyes search across the whole earth. He is looking for people whose hearts are fully loyal to him, so that he can make them strong. What you did was foolish. From now on you will always have wars.”
Asa became furious with the seer for saying this. He was so angry that he had Hanani locked up with his feet in wooden blocks. At the same time Asa began to treat some of the people cruelly.{f}
The full story of Asa’s reign, first to last, can be found in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.{g}
In the thirty-ninth year Asa was king, he got a disease in his feet. His sickness became very bad. But even when he was sick, he did not ask Yahweh for help. He went only to the doctors.{h}
In the forty-first year he was king, Asa died and joined his ancestors.

They placed his body in a tomb he had dug out of the rock for himself in David’s City. They laid him on a bed covered with sweet-smelling spices and perfumes, mixed by skilled perfume makers. Then they built a huge fire to honor him.{i}

notes.text: Verses 1-6 are much like 1 Kings 15:16-22. Ramah means “height.” See the note on 15:19.
Ben-hadad means “son of Hadad,” the storm god.
Ijon may mean “ruin.” Abel-maim means “meadow of waters.” 1 Kings 15:20 calls it Abel-beth-maacah. Naphtali means “my struggle.”
Geba means “hill.” Mizpah means “lookout tower.”
Hanani means “kind.” Verses 7-10 are not found in Kings.
The Hebrew says “the house of the stocks.” Stocks were heavy wooden frames that held a prisoner’s feet.
Compare 1 Kings 15:23-24.
Asa’s name may mean “healer,” so there may be a play on words here.
The fire was for burning spices to honor him. His body was not burned. Compare 21:19 and Jeremiah 34:5.

subheads.1: Asa Makes a Deal with Aram

verses.text: Asa’s son Jehoshaphat took the throne after him. He made his kingdom strong so it could stand against Israel.{a}
He stationed troops in every walled town of Judah. He set up army posts across Judah’s land and in the Ephraim towns that had fallen to his father Asa.
Yahweh stood by Jehoshaphat, who in his first years walked in the path his forefather David had taken. He refused to seek the Baal gods.{b}
Instead he looked to the God his father had worshiped and obeyed his commands. He did not act the way the people of Israel did.
So Yahweh made the kingdom secure under Jehoshaphat’s rule. All the people of Judah brought him gifts, and he became very rich and highly honored.
He was proud to follow Yahweh’s ways. He went on to remove the hilltop shrines and the Asherah poles from Judah.{c}
In his third year as king, Jehoshaphat sent out some of his officials to teach in Judah’s towns. Their names were Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel and Micaiah.{d}
Levites went with them: Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah and Tob-adonijah. Two priests also joined them, Elishama and Jehoram.{e}
They carried the book of Yahweh’s law with them and taught the people of Judah. They traveled from town to town all through Judah, teaching the people.
The kingdoms in the lands around Judah were filled with fear of Yahweh. So none of them went to war with Jehoshaphat.
Some Philistines brought gifts to Jehoshaphat and paid him silver as a tax. Arab herders brought him seven thousand seven hundred rams, and the same number of male goats.
Jehoshaphat kept growing more and more powerful. He built forts and towns for storing supplies throughout Judah.
He kept great stores of supplies in Judah’s towns. In Jerusalem he kept an army of trained, brave soldiers.
Here is how they were listed by families. From Judah came the commanders of units of a thousand. Adnah was the chief commander, over 300,000 brave soldiers.{f}
Next in command was Jehohanan, with 280,000 men.{g}
Next came Amasiah, Zichri’s son, who had volunteered to serve Yahweh. He led 200,000 brave soldiers.{h}
From Benjamin came Eliada, a brave soldier. He led 200,000 men armed with bows and shields.{i}
Next came Jehozabad, with 180,000 men ready for battle.{j}
These men all served the king. They were in addition to the troops he had placed in the walled towns all over Judah.

notes.text: Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.” Compare 1 Kings 15:24 and 22:41-50.

The Septuagint and some Hebrew copies do not have “David.” Then it would read “the early ways of his father,” meaning Asa. The Baals were local forms of the god Baal, whose name means “lord” or “owner.”
The Hebrew says “his heart was high.” Here it means he was bold and eager in a good way. Compare 20:33.
Ben-hail means “son of strength.” Obadiah means “servant of Yahweh.” Zechariah means “Yahweh remembers.”
Nethaniah means “Yahweh has given.” Adonijah means “my lord is Yahweh.” Tobijah means “Yahweh is good.” Elishama means “God has heard.” Jehoram means “Yahweh is lifted up.”
Adnah means “joy.” The total in verses 14-18 is 1,160,000, a very large number. See the note on 13:3.
Jehohanan means “Yahweh is kind.”
Amasiah means “Yahweh carries.” Zichri means “remembered.”
Eliada means “God knows.”
Jehozabad means “Yahweh has given.”

verses.text: Jehoshaphat was very rich and highly honored. He joined his family to Ahab’s family through marriage.{a}

Some years later Jehoshaphat went down to visit Ahab in Samaria. Ahab had many sheep and cattle butchered to feast Jehoshaphat and the men who came with him. Then Ahab tried to talk him into attacking Ramoth-gilead.{b}

Ahab, Israel’s king, asked Judah’s king Jehoshaphat, “Will you march with me against Ramoth-gilead?” Jehoshaphat answered, “You and I are one, and my troops are yours. Count on us to fight at your side.”
Jehoshaphat then said, “Before anything else, ask for a word from Yahweh.”
So Israel’s king brought together his prophets, four hundred of them. “Do we attack Ramoth-gilead,” he asked, “or do I wait?” “March!” they answered. “God will put the city in the king’s hands.”
Jehoshaphat, though, asked, “Is no other prophet of Yahweh around whom we could also consult?”

Israel’s king told Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man we could ask to find out Yahweh’s will. But I can’t stand him. He never says anything good about me. It’s always bad news. His name is Micaiah, Imla’s son.” Jehoshaphat said, “The king should not talk that way.”{c}
So Israel’s king called one of his officials and told him, “Hurry and get Micaiah, Imla’s son.”{d}

The two kings, Ahab of Israel and Jehoshaphat of Judah, were dressed in their royal robes. They sat on their thrones on the open threshing floor at the entrance to Samaria’s gate. All the prophets were acting out their messages in front of them.{e}
One of them, Zedekiah, Chenaanah’s son, had made a pair of iron horns. He announced, “Yahweh says, ‘With horns like these you will gore the Arameans until there are none left!’”{f}
All the other prophets agreed. “Attack Ramoth-gilead and win!” they said. “Yahweh will give it to the king!”
The messenger who went to bring Micaiah told him, “Listen, every one of the prophets is promising the king success. Please agree with them and say something good.”
But Micaiah answered, “I promise, as surely as Yahweh lives, I will say only what my God tells me.”
Micaiah came in, and the king asked, “Micaiah, do we attack Ramoth-gilead or do I wait?” “March up and win,” Micaiah replied. “They will be placed in your power.”
The king snapped at him, “How often must I put you under oath to speak only truth to me in Yahweh’s name?”
So Micaiah said, “I saw all Israel scattered over the hills like sheep with no shepherd. And Yahweh said, ‘These people have no master. Send each of them safely back home.’”
Then Israel’s king turned to Jehoshaphat. “What did I say? He never predicts anything good for me. Only trouble!”
Micaiah went on, “So hear what Yahweh says! I saw Yahweh seated on his throne. Heaven’s whole army stood about him on both sides.
Yahweh asked, ‘Who will trick Ahab, Israel’s king, into attacking Ramoth-gilead so he will be killed there?’ Some said one thing, and some said another.
At last a spirit stepped out and took his place before Yahweh. ‘I will trick him,’ the spirit said. ‘How will you do it?’ Yahweh asked.{g}
The spirit answered, ‘I will go out and put lies in the mouths of all his prophets.’ Yahweh said, ‘You will trick him, and it will work. Go and do it.’
“So now you see, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouths of these prophets of yours. Yahweh has announced disaster for you.”
Then Zedekiah, Chenaanah’s son, walked up and slapped Micaiah across the face. “And just when did Yahweh’s Spirit pass from me over to you?” he sneered.
“The day you go hiding in some inner room,” Micaiah replied, “you’ll know.”
Israel’s king ordered, “Arrest Micaiah! Hand him over to Amon, who governs the city, and to Prince Joash.{h}
Give them this order from the king: ‘Lock this man up. Give him nothing but a little bread and water until I come home safely.’”{i}
Micaiah said, “If you ever come home safely, then Yahweh has not spoken through me.” Then he added, “Remember what I said, all you people!”{j}
So Israel’s king and Jehoshaphat, Judah’s king, marched up to Ramoth-gilead.
Ahab told Jehoshaphat, “I will go into battle in disguise, but you wear your royal robes.” So Israel’s king disguised himself, and both kings headed into the fight.
Aram’s king had commanded his chariot officers: “Don’t fight anyone else, big or small. Attack only the king of Israel.”

When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they thought, “That’s Israel’s king!” They wheeled around to charge at him. Jehoshaphat screamed for help, and Yahweh came to his rescue. God turned the soldiers away from him.{k}
The commanders saw that he was not Israel’s king after all, so they stopped chasing him.

But one soldier shot an arrow without aiming at anyone in particular. It hit Israel’s king in a gap between the pieces of his armor. “Turn the chariot!” the king told his driver. “Take me away from the battle. I’m badly wounded!”{l}
The battle raged all day long. Israel’s king propped himself up in his chariot facing the Arameans until evening. As the sun was setting, he died.{m}

notes.text: Ahab means “father’s brother.” Jehoshaphat’s son Jehoram married Ahab’s daughter Athaliah (21:6; 22:2). This chapter is much like 1 Kings 22:1-35.
Samaria means “lookout.” Ramoth-gilead means “heights of Gilead.”
Micaiah means “who is like Yahweh?” Imla means “he fills.”
Some Hebrew copies spell the name Micaihu, a longer form.
Or “in an open place.”
Zedekiah means “Yahweh is right.” Chenaanah may mean “trader.”
The Hebrew says “With what?”
Amon may mean “faithful.” Joash may mean “Yahweh has given.”
The Hebrew says “bread of trouble and water of trouble,” meaning very small prison meals.
The same words begin the book of Micah (Micah 1:2).
The words “Yahweh came to his rescue. God turned the soldiers away” are not in 1 Kings 22:32.
The Hebrew says “out of the camp.”
1 Kings 22:35-38 adds that his blood ran into the chariot and that dogs licked it up in Samaria.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat, Judah’s king, made it home safe and sound to his palace in Jerusalem.

But the seer Jehu, Hanani’s son, came out to face him. He told King Jehoshaphat, “Is it right for you to help evil people and to be friends with those who hate Yahweh? Because you did this, Yahweh is angry with you.{a}
Still, some good is in you. You cleared the Asherah poles out of the land, and you made up your mind to follow God.”{b}

Jehoshaphat made Jerusalem his home. But he went out once more among his people. He traveled from Beersheba in the south to the hills of Ephraim in the north. Everywhere he went, he led them back to Yahweh, the God their forefathers worshiped.{c}
He placed judges throughout the land, one set for each walled town of Judah.{d}
He gave the judges this charge: “Be careful how you do your work. You are not judging for any human being. You judge for Yahweh, and he stands beside you each time you decide a case.
So let respect for Yahweh guide you. Watch what you do. Yahweh our God has no part in crooked deals. He never favors one side, and he never takes a bribe.”
In Jerusalem too, Jehoshaphat chose some Levites, priests, and leaders of Israel’s family clans. They were to judge cases for Yahweh and settle quarrels among the people. They lived in Jerusalem.{e}
He gave them orders: “Always act out of deep respect for Yahweh. Be honest, and give your whole heart to your work.

Your fellow Israelites in the towns will bring cases to you. Some will be about killings. Others will be about laws, rules, commands, or decisions. Each time, caution them so they don’t become guilty before Yahweh. If you fail to warn them, his anger will fall on you and on them. Do your job this way, and no blame will rest on you.{f}

“In all of Yahweh’s business, Amariah the high priest is your head. In all of the king’s business, Zebadiah, Ishmael’s son, leader of the tribe of Judah, is your head. The Levites will serve you as officers. Be brave and do your work. May Yahweh be with those who do right.”{g}

notes.text: Jehu means “Yahweh is he.” For Hanani, see 16:7.
The Hebrew word is Asheroth, the plural of Asherah. See the note at 14:3.
Beersheba means “well of seven” or “well of the promise.” Jehoshaphat’s own name means “Yahweh has judged,” which fits the changes he made in the courts (verses 5-11).
See Deuteronomy 16:18-20 and 17:8-13.
The Hebrew says “and they returned to Jerusalem.” The Greek translation reads “to judge the people living in Jerusalem,” which comes from reading the same Hebrew letters a different way.
The Hebrew says “between blood and blood,” meaning cases of murder and bloodshed.
Amariah means “Yahweh has said.” For Zebadiah, see 17:8. Ishmael means “God hears.”

verses.text: After these things, Moab’s and Ammon’s armies, joined by some Meunites, set out to fight Jehoshaphat.{a}

Messengers came to Jehoshaphat with a report. “A massive army is on its way to fight you,” they said. “It is coming from Aram, from the far side of the Dead Sea. It has already reached Hazazon-tamar.” (Hazazon-tamar is another name for En-gedi.){b}
Fear gripped Jehoshaphat, and he decided to turn to Yahweh. He called a fast for everyone in Judah.
People from every town in Judah came together. They all came to ask Yahweh to help them.
Jehoshaphat stood up in front of the gathered people of Judah and Jerusalem. He stood at Yahweh’s temple, facing the new courtyard.
He prayed, “Yahweh, God of our forefathers, you are God who lives in heaven! You rule every kingdom of every nation. You are strong and mighty. Nobody can hold out against you.
Our God, it was you who pushed out this land’s earlier peoples so your people Israel could have it. You handed it over to the family of your friend Abraham to keep for all time.{c}
Our people settled here. They built a temple here to honor your name. Then they declared,

‘Disaster may strike us, whether war, a judgment, plague, or famine. When that happens, we will stand at this temple that bears your name, standing in your presence. We will call out to you in our misery, and you will listen and save us.’{d}

“Now look at the armies coming from Ammon, Moab, and the hills of Seir! When Israel came out of Egypt long ago, you would not let our people invade those lands. So Israel went around them and left them alone.{e}
Now see how they pay us back! They mean to throw us off the land you let us inherit.
Our God, won’t you punish them? This vast army marching on us is far too strong for us. We have no plan. Our eyes are fixed on you.”
Judah’s men, their wives, their children, and even their little babies stood there together before Yahweh.

Then Yahweh’s Spirit came on a man in the crowd named Jahaziel. This Levite belonged to Asaph’s family line. His father was Zechariah. His grandfather was Benaiah, and before him came Jeiel and Mattaniah.{f}
