Jahaziel said, “Pay attention, King Jehoshaphat and all you people of Judah and Jerusalem! Yahweh has this message for you: ‘Stop being afraid. Don’t lose heart because of this huge army. This is God’s fight, not yours.
Tomorrow, march down to meet them. They will be climbing up through the Ziz Pass. You will find them at the far end of the valley that faces the Jeruel wilderness.{g}

You will not have to fight at all. Just take your places and stand there. Watch how Yahweh will save you, Judah and Jerusalem.’ So don’t be afraid or lose heart. Go out to face them tomorrow. Yahweh will be there with you.”{h}
Jehoshaphat bowed down low with his face on the ground. All the people of Judah and Jerusalem bowed down too and worshiped Yahweh.
Next, Levites of the Kohath and Korah clans rose to their feet. They praised Yahweh, the God of Israel, shouting as loudly as they could.{i}

The people got up early the next morning and headed out to the Tekoa wilderness. As they were leaving, Jehoshaphat stood and called out, “Hear me, Judah and Jerusalem! Trust Yahweh your God, and nothing will shake you. Believe his prophets, and you will win.”{j}

After talking with the people, Jehoshaphat chose men to sing to Yahweh. They were to march in front of the soldiers, praising him for his holy beauty. They sang, “Thank Yahweh! His faithful love lasts forever!”{k}
The moment they started singing and praising, Yahweh set traps for the armies of Ammon, Moab, and Seir that were invading Judah. The enemy was beaten.
The Ammonites and Moabites turned on the men from Seir and wiped them out completely. When they had finished them off, they began killing each other.
Judah’s army came to the lookout point in the desert. They gazed toward the vast enemy force. Corpses covered the ground everywhere. Not one enemy soldier had escaped.

Jehoshaphat and his men went down to collect the goods the enemy left behind. They found large amounts of supplies, clothing, and valuable things, far too much to haul away. For three whole days they gathered it, because there was so much.{l}
On the fourth day they met in a valley and praised Yahweh there. That is why it is still named Beracah Valley, which means “Blessing Valley.”{m}
Then all the men of Judah and Jerusalem headed back home to Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat leading them. They were full of joy, because Yahweh had let them triumph over their foes.
They marched into Jerusalem and up to Yahweh’s temple playing harps, lyres, and trumpets.
All the kingdoms around heard how Yahweh had fought Israel’s enemies. They became terrified of God.
So Jehoshaphat’s kingdom had peace. His God gave him rest from enemies on every side.
Jehoshaphat ruled over Judah. At thirty-five he became king, and his rule in Jerusalem lasted twenty-five years. Azubah was his mother, and Shilhi was her father.{n}
He lived as his father Asa had lived and never turned away from that path. He did what Yahweh saw as right.
Even so, the hilltop shrines were left standing. The people had still not set their hearts firmly on their forefathers’ God.{o}
You can read about everything else Jehoshaphat did, from start to finish, in the record of Jehu, Hanani’s son. It was copied into the book about Israel’s kings.
Later on, Jehoshaphat, Judah’s king, made a deal with Ahaziah, Israel’s king, a very evil man.{p}
The two of them agreed to build trading ships to sail to Tarshish. They built the ships at Ezion-geber.{q}

Then a man from Mareshah named Eliezer, Dodavahu’s son, spoke a prophecy against Jehoshaphat. “You partnered with Ahaziah,” he said, “so Yahweh will wreck what you have built.” The ships were smashed and never sailed to Tarshish.{r}

notes.text: The Hebrew says “some of the Ammonites,” which repeats the Ammonites already named. The Greek translation reads “Minaeans,” meaning Meunites (see 26:7). For Moab, see the note at 1 Chronicles 1:46. Ammon means “people.”

The Hebrew and Greek say “from Aram.” Many experts read “from Edom,” since the two words look very much alike in Hebrew and the attackers came from the south, around the Dead Sea. The Hebrew says simply “the sea.” Hazazon-tamar may mean “gravel bed of the palm tree.” En-gedi means “spring of the young goat.”
See Isaiah 41:8 and James 2:23.
See Solomon’s prayer in 6:28-30.
Seir means “hairy,” and it is the hill country of Edom. See Deuteronomy 2:4-19.
Jahaziel means “God sees.” Benaiah means “Yahweh has built.” The meaning of Jeiel is not known. Mattaniah means “gift of Yahweh.” Asaph means “gatherer.”
Ziz may mean “blossom.” Jeruel may mean “founded by God.” The Hebrew says “before,” meaning to the east.
See Exodus 14:13.
The Kohathites came from Kohath, a name that may mean “gathering.” The Korahites came from Korah, which may mean “bald.”
Tekoa may mean “trumpet blast.” “Put your faith ... stand strong” is a word play on two forms of the same Hebrew word. See Isaiah 7:9.
Or “dressed in holy clothes.” “Faithful love” is the Hebrew word hesed.
Many Hebrew copies say “dead bodies.” Some experts read “clothing,” which differs by one Hebrew letter. The Greek translation reads “cattle and furniture and spoils.”
Beracah means “blessing.”
Verses 31-34 are much like 1 Kings 22:41-45. Azubah means “left alone.” Shilhi may mean “sent.”

1 Kings 22:43 says people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the hilltop shrines. In 17:6 Jehoshaphat removed hilltop shrines. The two verses may speak of different kinds of shrines or different times in his rule.
Ahaziah means “Yahweh has taken hold.” Or “and he (Jehoshaphat) did wrong by doing this.”

Tarshish was a faraway port in the west (see the note at 9:21). 1 Kings 22:48-49 says Jehoshaphat built “Tarshish ships” (a kind of large ocean ship) to go to Ophir for gold, and that he turned down Ahaziah’s offer to join him. Chronicles may have understood “Tarshish ships” as ships going to Tarshish. Ezion-geber was on the Red Sea, not the Mediterranean. Its name may mean “backbone of a man.”
Eliezer means “God is help.” Dodavahu means “loved by Yahweh.” This prophecy is not in Kings.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat died and joined his forefathers. He was laid in their family tomb in David’s City, and his son Jehoram took the throne after him.{a}
Jehoshaphat had other sons too, Jehoram’s brothers: Michael, Shephatiah, Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah and Azariahu. All six were sons of Jehoshaphat, Israel’s king.{b}
Their father had handed them generous gifts of silver, gold and other treasures, plus walled towns in Judah. But the crown went to Jehoram, since he was the oldest son.
Once Jehoram had his father’s kingdom firmly under control, he put every one of his brothers to death with the sword. Some of Israel’s leaders died with them.
Jehoram became king at thirty-two. For eight years he ruled from Jerusalem.{c}
He copied the kings of Israel, just as Ahab’s family did, since his wife was Ahab’s daughter. In Yahweh’s eyes, what he did was evil.
Yet Yahweh was unwilling to wipe out David’s royal line, because of the covenant he had made with David. He had promised that a lamp would keep burning for David and his sons for all time.{d}
While Jehoram was king, Edom broke free from Judah’s rule and crowned a king of its own.
So Jehoram crossed over with his officers and every chariot he had. The Edomites surrounded him and his chariot captains, but he got up in the night and broke through their lines.{e}
Edom has stayed free of Judah’s control ever since. Libnah broke away from his rule about the same time. This happened because Jehoram had turned away from Yahweh, the God his forefathers served.{f}
He even built hilltop shrines in the hills of Judah. He led Jerusalem’s people to be unfaithful to God, and he pulled Judah off the right path.{g}

Then a letter reached Jehoram from Elijah the prophet. It said: “Here is the message of Yahweh, the God your forefather David served: ‘Your father Jehoshaphat walked a good road, and so did Asa, who ruled Judah before him. You have not.{h}

Instead, you have followed the path of Israel’s kings. You have led Judah and the people in Jerusalem to be unfaithful to me, the way Ahab’s family did. You also murdered your own brothers, your father’s sons, men who were better than you.
Now watch! Yahweh is about to bring a terrible blow on your people, your sons, your wives, and everything you own.
You yourself will become very sick with a disease in your bowels. It will get worse day after day, until your insides come out.’”
Yahweh stirred up the Philistines against Jehoram. He also stirred up the Arabs who lived next to the Cushites.{i}
These armies marched up, invaded Judah and smashed their way in. They hauled off all the riches in the king’s palace, even his wives and sons. Only one son was left to him, his youngest, Jehoahaz.{j}
After all of this happened, Yahweh struck Jehoram with a sickness in his bowels that could not be cured.

It dragged on, and two years later his insides came out because of the illness. He died in terrible agony. His people did not light a great fire to honor him, as they had done for the kings before him.{k}

Jehoram had been thirty-two when he started to rule, and he ruled eight years in Jerusalem. When he died, no one was sorry. He was buried in David’s City, but they did not put him in the royal tombs.{l}

notes.text: Jehoram means “Yahweh is lifted high.” He is also called Joram. Verses 1 and 5-10 are much like 2 Kings 8:16-22.

Azariah and Azariahu are two forms of a name that means “Yahweh has helped.” Jehiel means “God lives.” Michael means “who is like God?” Shephatiah means “Yahweh has judged.” Here “king of Israel” means king of Judah, which Chronicles sees as the true Israel. The Greek translation reads “king of Judah.”
Jehoram may have ruled for some years together with his father (see 2 Kings 1:17; 3:1; 8:16).
The “lamp” means a living son of David on the throne (see 1 Kings 11:36).
2 Kings 8:21 says Joram went over to Zair and that his army ran away home. It was an escape, not a victory.
Libnah means “whiteness.” It was a town in the low hills near Philistia.
The Greek translation reads “in the towns of Judah.” The Hebrew says “caused them to commit sexual sin,” which pictures turning from Yahweh to idols.

Elijah means “my God is Yahweh.” Elijah is not linked with Jehoram of Judah anywhere else. 2 Kings 2-3 seems to show Elijah leaving the earth before Jehoram’s rule (Elisha is already working under Jehoshaphat, 2 Kings 3:11). Elijah may have written the letter ahead of time, or he may have lived into the early years when Jehoram ruled with his father. Experts disagree.
For Cush, see 12:3.
Jehoahaz means “Yahweh has taken hold.” It has the same parts as the name Ahaziah (22:1), but in reverse order.
The Hebrew says “in severe diseases.” For the fire, see the note at 16:14.
The detail that he was not put in the royal tombs is not in Kings (see 2 Kings 8:24).

verses.text: Jerusalem’s people crowned Ahaziah, Jehoram’s youngest son, as the next king. The raiders who came into the camp with the Arabs had killed all of his older brothers. So Ahaziah, Jehoram’s son, began to rule Judah.{a}
Ahaziah was twenty-two when he took the throne, and he lasted only one year as king in Jerusalem. His mother, Athaliah, came from Omri’s family.{b}
He too lived like Ahab’s family did. His mother kept giving him wicked advice.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, like Ahab’s family. After his father died, they became his advisers, and their advice ruined him.
Following their advice, he joined Joram, Ahab’s son, the king of Israel, in a war against Hazael, Aram’s king, at Ramoth-gilead. There the Arameans wounded Joram.{c}

Joram went back to Jezreel to heal from the wounds he got at Ramah while fighting King Hazael of Aram. Ahaziah, Jehoram’s son and Judah’s king, traveled down to Jezreel to see how Joram, Ahab’s son, was doing, since he was still hurt.{d}
God used this visit to bring Ahaziah down. When he got there, he rode out with Joram to meet Jehu, Nimshi’s son. Yahweh had anointed Jehu to wipe out Ahab’s family.{e}
While Jehu was carrying out judgment on Ahab’s family, he came across some of Judah’s leaders and the sons of Ahaziah’s relatives who served Ahaziah. Jehu killed them.{f}

Then Jehu hunted for Ahaziah. His men found him hiding in Samaria and dragged him to Jehu, who had him killed. They gave him a burial. “His grandfather was Jehoshaphat,” they said, “a man who sought Yahweh with his whole heart.” No one in Ahaziah’s family was left strong enough to rule the kingdom.{g}
When word reached Athaliah, Ahaziah’s mother, that her son had been killed, she set out to kill off the whole royal family of Judah.{h}

But Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram’s daughter, rescued Ahaziah’s baby son Joash. She snatched him from among the king’s sons who were marked for death and hid him with his nurse in a bedroom. Jehoshabeath was the sister of Ahaziah, and she was married to Jehoiada the priest. Because she hid the boy, Athaliah never found him to kill him.{i}
For six years Joash stayed hidden with them at God’s temple, while Athaliah ruled the land.

notes.text: Ahaziah means “Yahweh has taken hold.” He is also called Jehoahaz (21:17). Verses 1-6 are much like 2 Kings 8:24-29.

The Hebrew here says “forty-two,” which cannot be right if his father died at forty (21:20). 2 Kings 8:26 says “twenty-two,” and the Greek translation here says “twenty.” Athaliah means “Yahweh is lifted high.” The meaning of Omri is not known. The Hebrew calls her Omri’s “daughter,” in the wider sense. She was Ahab’s daughter (21:6).
Hazael means “God sees.”
Ramah is a short form of Ramoth-gilead. The Hebrew says “Azariah,” but the Greek translation and 2 Kings 8:29 say “Ahaziah,” which is surely correct (see verses 1 and 7). Jezreel means “God plants.”
For Jehu, see 19:2. Nimshi may mean “weasel.” See 2 Kings 9-10.
2 Kings 10:12-14 calls them “Ahaziah’s relatives” and says there were forty-two of them.

2 Kings 9:27-28 says Ahaziah was wounded near Ibleam, fled to Megiddo and died there. His servants carried him to Jerusalem to be buried. Chronicles tells it more briefly and differently. The two reports may come from different sources or describe different parts of his escape.
Verses 10-12 are much like 2 Kings 11:1-3.
Jehoshabeath means “Yahweh is a promise.” 2 Kings 11:2 calls her Jehosheba. For Joash, see 18:25. Jehoiada means “Yahweh knows.” Only Chronicles says she was Jehoiada’s wife.

verses.text: In the seventh year, Jehoiada found his courage. He made a binding agreement with five army officers, each in charge of a hundred men. They were Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.{a}
These officers went all through Judah. In every town they gathered the Levites and the leaders of Israel’s family clans and brought them to Jerusalem.

There at God’s temple, the whole crowd made a covenant with the young king. Jehoiada told them, “Here is the king’s son! He is the one who must rule, just as Yahweh promised about David’s descendants.
Here is your plan. You priests and Levites who start your duty on the Sabbath will split into three groups. One group will guard the temple doors.{b}
Another group will guard the palace. The last group will guard the Foundation Gate. Everyone else must stay in the courtyards of Yahweh’s temple.{c}

Don’t let anyone into Yahweh’s temple but the priests and those Levites serving their shift. Only they may enter, because they are set apart as holy. All the other people must obey Yahweh’s rules and stay outside.{d}
The Levites must form a ring around the king, every man holding his weapons. Kill anyone else who tries to come into the temple. Stay at the king’s side wherever he goes.”

The Levites and all of Judah carried out every order Jehoiada the priest gave. Each officer took his men, both those starting their Sabbath shift and those finishing it, because Jehoiada had not let any of the groups go home.
Then Jehoiada handed the officers the spears and the big and small shields that once belonged to King David. These had been kept in God’s temple.

He placed all the men, each one gripping his weapon, around the king. Their line stretched across the temple courtyard, from its right-hand side over to its left, close by the altar and the temple building.

Then Jehoiada and his sons led out the king’s son. They put the crown on his head and handed him a copy of God’s covenant laws. They made him king and poured oil on his head. “Long live the king!” everyone shouted.{e}
The sound of people rushing about and cheering the king reached Athaliah. So she came to Yahweh’s temple where the crowd was.

There she saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance. The officers and trumpet players were next to him. The common people were full of joy, sounding trumpets. Singers with instruments were leading everyone in praise. Athaliah ripped her clothes and screamed, “Traitors! Traitors!”{f}

Jehoiada the priest called out the army officers who commanded the hundreds. “March her out between your lines,” he told them. “Kill anyone who comes after her.” He had said, “Don’t kill her inside Yahweh’s temple.”
So they grabbed her as she reached the Horse Gate entrance at the palace, and that is where she died.{g}
Next, Jehoiada had the king, the people and himself agree together in a covenant. They promised to be Yahweh’s people.
Then the whole crowd went to Baal’s temple and tore it down. They smashed his altars and statues to bits. They killed Mattan, Baal’s priest, in front of the altars.{h}

Jehoiada put the Levite priests in charge of Yahweh’s temple, just as David had divided their work long before. They were to offer burnt offerings to Yahweh as the Law of Moses says. They were to do it with joy and singing, as David had ordered.
He placed guards at the gates of Yahweh’s temple. They were to keep out anyone who was unclean for any reason.

He gathered the army officers, the important men, the leaders of the people and all the people of the land. Together they led the king down from Yahweh’s temple. Passing through the Upper Gate, they entered the royal house and seated him on his throne.
Joy filled everyone across the land. With Athaliah dead by the sword, the city became calm.

notes.text: Chapter 23 is much like 2 Kings 11:4-20. Chronicles gives the names of the five officers and gives the Levites a larger part. For Azariah, see 15:1. Jeroham means “he is shown kindness.” For Ishmael, see 19:11. For Jehohanan, see 17:15. Obed means “servant.” Maaseiah means “work of Yahweh.” Adaiah means “Yahweh has decorated.” Elishaphat means “God has judged.” For Zichri, see 17:16.
The Hebrew says “of the thresholds,” meaning the temple doorways.
2 Kings 11:6 says “the Sur Gate.”
This means they must stay in the outer courtyards, as Yahweh requires.
The Hebrew says “the testimony.” This may have been a copy of the covenant law (see Deuteronomy 17:18) or some royal paper.
The Hebrew says “Conspiracy! Conspiracy!”
The Hebrew says “they made two sides for her,” which may mean they opened a path for her or took hold of her.
Mattan means “gift.”

verses.text: Joash was a boy of seven when he became king. He ruled from Jerusalem for forty years. His mother, Zibiah, came from Beersheba.{a}
As long as Jehoiada the priest was alive, Joash did what pleased Yahweh.
Jehoiada picked out two wives for him, and Joash had sons and daughters.
Some time later, Joash set his heart on fixing up Yahweh’s temple.{b}

He called the priests and Levites together. “Travel through the towns of Judah,” he told them. “Every year, gather money from all the Israelites to keep your God’s temple in good repair. Do it quickly!” But the Levites dragged their feet.

So the king sent for Jehoiada, the head priest. “Why haven’t you made the Levites collect the tax from Judah and Jerusalem?” he asked. “Moses, Yahweh’s servant, and the people of Israel set up that tax for the Tent of God’s covenant laws.”{c}
Athaliah, that evil woman, and her sons had broken into God’s temple. They had even taken the holy objects from Yahweh’s temple and used them to worship the Baal gods.{d}
So the king gave an order, and workers built a wooden chest. They set it outside, by the gate of Yahweh’s temple.
Word was spread throughout Judah and Jerusalem. Everyone was to bring Yahweh the tax that God’s servant Moses had required of Israel back in the wilderness.
Leaders and common people alike gladly brought their gifts. They kept dropping their money into the chest until it was full.

From time to time the Levites would carry the chest to the king’s officials. When the officials saw it held a lot of money, the king’s secretary and the head priest’s helper came. They emptied out the chest and then carried it back to its spot. They did this again and again and gathered a great pile of money.

The king and Jehoiada passed the money along to the men who managed the temple work. These men hired stone cutters and woodworkers to rebuild Yahweh’s temple. They also paid men skilled at working iron and bronze to fix it.
The workers kept busy, and the repairs moved ahead under their care. They made God’s temple as strong and good as it had been at first.

When the work was done, they took the leftover money to the king and Jehoiada. With it they made things for Yahweh’s temple: objects for the service and for the burnt offerings, small dishes, and other gold and silver items. Burnt offerings were given in Yahweh’s temple day after day for as long as Jehoiada lived.{e}
Jehoiada lived a long, full life. He was 130 when he died.{f}
They buried him among the kings in David’s City. He had served Israel well, and he had served God and God’s house.
Once Jehoiada was dead, Judah’s officials came to honor the king with deep bows, and Joash began to heed what they said.
They turned their backs on the temple of Yahweh, their forefathers’ God. Instead they served idols and the poles of Asherah. Their guilt brought God’s anger down on Judah and Jerusalem.
Yahweh kept sending prophets to them to bring them back to him. Again and again the prophets spoke out against them, yet no one paid attention.

Then God’s Spirit came over Zechariah, the son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood up where the people could see him and said, “Here is God’s message: ‘Why are you breaking Yahweh’s commands? You will never do well this way! You turned your backs on Yahweh, so he has turned his back on you.’”{g}
But a plot was formed against Zechariah. On the king’s command they stoned him to death, right in the courtyard of Yahweh’s temple.
King Joash forgot how loyal and kind Jehoiada, Zechariah’s father, had been to him. He killed Jehoiada’s son anyway. As Zechariah lay dying, he cried out, “May Yahweh see this and make you pay!”{h}
In the spring, Aram’s army came to attack Joash. They invaded Judah and Jerusalem, and they killed all the people’s leaders. They sent everything they captured to their king in Damascus.{i}
Aram’s army was small, but Yahweh let it defeat Judah’s far bigger army. This was because Judah had deserted Yahweh, the God their forefathers knew. In this way, Joash was punished.

The Arameans pulled back, leaving Joash badly wounded. Then his own officials made a plot to kill him, because he had murdered the son of Jehoiada the priest. While Joash lay on his bed, they struck him dead. His grave was in David’s City, though he was left out of the tombs of the kings.{j}
The men who plotted against him were Zabad and Jehozabad. Zabad’s mother, Shimeath, was an Ammonite woman. Jehozabad’s mother, Shimrith, was a Moabite woman.{k}

What happened to Joash’s sons, the many warnings spoken against him, and how he rebuilt God’s temple are all recorded in the notes on the book of the kings. After him the crown passed to his son Amaziah.{l}

notes.text: Joash is also called Jehoash. See 18:25. Zibiah means “gazelle.” Verses 1-14 are much like 2 Kings 12:1-16, which tells about the collection a bit differently.
The Hebrew says “it was in the heart of Joash.”
See Exodus 30:12-16. That tax was half a shekel, about one-fifth of an ounce of silver.
The Hebrew says “her sons,” which may mean her followers. Or “had torn down God’s temple.”
The Hebrew word means small pans used for incense. 2 Kings 12:13 says the money was not used for such objects. Chronicles may mean the money left over after the repairs.
Jehoiada lived longer than Moses or Aaron.

The Hebrew says “God’s Spirit clothed itself with Zechariah” (see Judges 6:34). For Zechariah, see 17:7. Jesus seems to speak of this murder in Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51. Matthew calls him “son of Barachiah” (see Zechariah 1:1).
Or “May Yahweh see and get justice.” See 2 Kings 12:17-18, which tells of Aram’s threat and the payment Joash made.
The Hebrew says “at the turn of the year,” meaning spring, when kings went to war (1 Chronicles 20:1).
The Hebrew says “sons.” The Greek translation reads “son.” 2 Kings 12:20-21 says he died at the house of Millo.

Zabad means “he has given.” 2 Kings 12:21 calls him Jozacar, “Yahweh has remembered.” Shimeath means “hearing.” For Jehozabad, see 17:18. Shimrith means “guard.” 2 Kings 12:21 has Shomer, a man’s name that also means “guard.” Kings does not say the mothers were from Ammon and Moab.
Hebrew copies spell the word for “many” in two slightly different ways. Amaziah means “Yahweh is strong.”

verses.text: At twenty-five Amaziah took the throne. Jerusalem was his royal city for twenty-nine years. Jehoaddan, a woman of Jerusalem, was his mother.{a}
He did what Yahweh saw as right, but his heart was not fully devoted.
As soon as he had a firm grip on the kingdom, he put to death the servants who had assassinated the king, his father.

But he spared the killers’ children. He obeyed what is written in the Law, in Moses’ book, where Yahweh commanded: “No father is to be executed for his son’s crime, and no son for his father’s crime. Each one pays with his life only for his own sin.”{b}

Amaziah called the men of Judah together. He arranged all of Judah and Benjamin by family clans and placed officers over groups of a thousand and groups of a hundred. He counted the men aged twenty and older. There were 300,000 of the best fighters, ready for war and skilled with spear and shield.
On top of that, he paid about three and three-quarter tons of silver to hire a hundred thousand of Israel’s mighty warriors.{c}
That is when a man of God arrived with a warning. “O king,” he said, “do not let Israel’s army march with you. Yahweh is not with Israel, not with any of those Ephraimites.
Even if you go and fight bravely, God will make you fall before your enemy. God has the power both to help and to bring down.”{d}
Amaziah questioned the man of God: “And my hundred talents? I’ve already handed them to Israel’s troops!” “Yahweh can repay you many times over,” came the reply.
So Amaziah dismissed the troops who had come from Ephraim and sent them home. Judah’s treatment made them furious, and they went home burning with rage.
Then Amaziah gathered his courage and led his army out. At the Valley of Salt they cut down ten thousand Seirites.{e}
Judah’s army also captured ten thousand men alive. They took them to the top of a cliff and threw them off, and every one of them was dashed to pieces.{f}

Meanwhile the hired troops Amaziah had sent home, the ones he would not let fight with him, attacked Judah’s towns. They raided everything from Samaria to Beth-horon, leaving three thousand dead and hauling away great heaps of loot.{g}
After Amaziah came back from slaughtering the Edomites, he brought along the gods of Seir’s people. He set them up as his own gods, bowed to them and burned incense for them.
This made Yahweh burn with anger against Amaziah. He sent a prophet, who asked him, “Why would you turn to these people’s gods? Those gods failed to rescue their own nation from your hand!”

While the prophet was still speaking, the king cut him off. “When did we make you a royal adviser? Stop! Do you want to be killed?” So the prophet fell silent, though not before adding, “It’s clear to me now: God plans to destroy you. You did this, and you would not take my advice.”{h}

Amaziah, Judah’s king, talked it over with his advisers. Then he sent a challenge to Israel’s king Joash, the son of Jehoahaz and grandson of Jehu. “Come,” he said, “let’s face each other in battle.”{i}

But Joash, Israel’s king, sent back this answer to Amaziah, Judah’s king: “Once a thornbush in Lebanon sent word to a cedar in Lebanon. ‘Let your daughter marry my son,’ it said. But then a wild animal of Lebanon came along and stomped the thornbush flat.{j}
You keep saying, ‘Look, I beat Edom!’ Now you are proud and want to brag. Stay at home! Why ask for trouble? It will only bring you down, and Judah will fall with you.”{k}
Amaziah would not listen. God was behind this, because he planned to hand Judah over to their enemies. They had gone after Edom’s gods.
So King Joash of Israel marched out, and the two kings faced off in battle at Beth-shemesh in Judah.{l}
Israel crushed Judah’s army, and every soldier of Judah ran home.

At Beth-shemesh, Joash, Israel’s king, captured Amaziah, Judah’s king, the son of Joash and grandson of Jehoahaz. Joash brought him to Jerusalem. He knocked down a section of the city wall six hundred feet long, all the way from Ephraim Gate over to Corner Gate.{m}

He grabbed all the gold and silver and every object he found in God’s temple, which Obed-edom’s family looked after. He took the palace treasures and some hostages too. Then he went back to Samaria.{n}
Amaziah son of Joash, Judah’s king, outlived Israel’s king Joash son of Jehoahaz by fifteen years.
Everything else Amaziah did, from first to last, is written in the book about the kings of Judah and Israel.
From the time Amaziah stopped following Yahweh, people in Jerusalem plotted against him. He escaped to Lachish, yet the plotters had men chase him down and kill him in that town.{o}
They carried his body back on horses and buried him with his forefathers in Judah’s city.{p}

notes.text: For Amaziah, see 24:27. Jehoaddan means “Yahweh is delight.” Verses 1-4 are much like 2 Kings 14:1-6. Verses 17-28 are much like 2 Kings 14:8-20.
See Deuteronomy 24:16.
The Hebrew says “a hundred talents.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds. So this was about 7,500 pounds of silver. Verses 5-16 are not in Kings.
The Hebrew here is hard to understand. Some read it, “If you go thinking you are strong for battle, God will make you fall.”
The Valley of Salt was probably south of the Dead Sea. 2 Kings 14:7 says Amaziah also captured Sela, a name meaning “rock.”
The Hebrew word for “cliff” is sela, which may point to Sela, Edom’s mountain fortress (2 Kings 14:7).
Beth-horon means “house of the hollow.”
The Hebrew word for “advice” or “adviser” is used several times in verses 16-17, a word play.
Joash, Israel’s king, is also called Jehoash. For Jehoahaz, see 21:17. For Jehu, see 19:2. Hebrew copies have an extra word here that is written and read slightly differently.
Lebanon means “white,” because of its snowy mountain tops.
The Hebrew says “You say, ‘Look, you have struck Edom.’” See 2 Kings 14:10.
Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.”
The Hebrew says “four hundred cubits.” A cubit was about eighteen inches.
Obed-edom means “servant of Edom.” His family were gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 26:15). Kings does not mention this detail (verse 24).
The meaning of Lachish is not known.
The Greek translation and 2 Kings 14:20 say “in David’s City.”

verses.text: Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah, a sixteen-year-old, and crowned him king to follow his father Amaziah.{a}
After his father the king died and was buried with his forefathers, Uzziah rebuilt Elath and won it back for Judah.{b}
Uzziah was sixteen when his rule began, and it lasted fifty-two years in Jerusalem. Jecoliah, a Jerusalem woman, was his mother.{c}
Like his father Amaziah, he did what Yahweh saw as right.
While Zechariah was alive, Uzziah made a point of seeking God. Zechariah taught him to understand God’s visions. As long as Uzziah looked to Yahweh, God made him successful.{d}
Uzziah went to war against the Philistines. He knocked down the walls of Gath, Jabneh and Ashdod. Then he built towns near Ashdod and in other parts of Philistine land.{e}
God gave him help in his wars with the Philistines, with the Meunites, and with Arabs who lived at Gur-baal.{f}
Ammon sent Uzziah tribute payments. He became so powerful that people heard about him all the way to the border of Egypt.
In Jerusalem, Uzziah built strong towers at three places: by the Corner Gate, by the Valley Gate, and where the wall turns.

Out in the desert he also put up towers and dug lots of water pits, for he kept large herds of animals in the western hills and on the flatlands. He loved working the soil, so he had people farming his fields and tending his vineyards in the hills and the rich valleys.{g}

Uzziah kept a well-trained army ready for battle. It went out in units. Jeiel, the royal secretary, and Maaseiah, an officer, mustered and listed the troops, working under Hananiah, a commander for the king.{h}
The family leaders in charge of these brave fighters numbered 2,600 in all.
These leaders commanded three hundred seven thousand five hundred soldiers. It was a powerful fighting force, ready to help the king against any enemy.
Uzziah equipped every soldier with shield and spear, helmet and armor coat, bow and sling stones.

In Jerusalem he had clever men design war machines. These were placed on the towers and on the corners of the walls to shoot arrows and hurl big stones. Uzziah became famous far and wide, because God helped him in amazing ways until he grew strong.{i}
But once Uzziah grew strong, he became proud, and his pride ruined him. He sinned against Yahweh his God. He entered Yahweh’s holy house intending to offer incense himself on its altar.{j}
Azariah the priest followed him inside. Eighty other brave priests of Yahweh went in with him.{k}

They stood up to King Uzziah. “It’s not your job, Uzziah, to offer incense to Yahweh!” they told him. “That job belongs only to the priests, Aaron’s descendants, who have been set apart to burn incense. Leave this holy place! You have broken faith, and this will bring you no glory from Yahweh God.”{l}

Uzziah was holding a pan for burning incense, and he became furious. As he raged at the priests, right there in Yahweh’s temple beside the incense altar, his forehead suddenly broke out with a skin disease while the priests watched.{m}

Azariah the high priest and the other priests stared at him. They saw the disease on his forehead, and they rushed him out of the temple. In fact, Uzziah himself hurried to get out, for the blow had come from Yahweh.

Uzziah carried that disease to his grave. Because of it, he lived alone in a separate house, and he was not allowed into Yahweh’s temple. Meanwhile his son Jotham ran the royal household and served as judge for the nation.{n}
Isaiah the prophet, Amoz’s son, wrote down everything else Uzziah did, from beginning to end.{o}

Uzziah died and joined his forefathers. They buried him near his forefathers in a field of graves that belonged to the kings, but not in the tombs themselves. Their reason was, “His skin was diseased.” The next king was Jotham, Uzziah’s son.{p}

notes.text: Uzziah means “Yahweh is my strength.” In 2 Kings 14:21; 15:1-7 and 1 Chronicles 3:12 he is called Azariah, “Yahweh has helped.” Verses 1-4 are much like 2 Kings 14:21-22 and 15:2-3.
Elath, also called Eloth, means “large trees” or “palm trees.” It was at the north tip of the Gulf of Aqaba.
Jecoliah means “Yahweh is able.” Hebrew copies spell this name in two slightly different ways.
For Zechariah, see 17:7. The Hebrew says “in the seeing of God.” The Greek translation and some Hebrew copies say “in the fear of God,” which differs by one letter.
Gath means “winepress.” Jabneh means “he builds,” and it was later called Jamnia. The meaning of Ashdod is not known.
Gur-baal may mean “home of Baal.” The Greek translation says “on the rock.” For the Meunites, see the note at 20:1. The Greek translation reads “Minaeans.”
The Hebrew says “the Shephelah,” the low hills west of Judah’s mountains. Or “because he loved the land.”
For Jeiel, see 20:14. For Maaseiah, see 23:1. Hananiah means “Yahweh has been kind.”
These may have been catapults, or covered shelters on the walls where archers and slingers could shoot from.
Verses 16-21 tell more than 2 Kings 15:5, which does not say why the disease came.
For Azariah, see 15:1.
See Numbers 16:40 and 18:1-7.
The Hebrew word tsaraat is used for many skin diseases, not only the disease called leprosy today. It made a person unclean for worship (Leviticus 13). Older English Bibles say “leprosy.”
The Hebrew says “a house of freedom.” This may mean a house set apart for the sick, or a house where he was freed from his duties. Jotham means “Yahweh is perfect.”
Isaiah means “Yahweh saves.” Amoz means “strong.” See Isaiah 1:1 and 6:1. This writing of Isaiah’s is not known today.
See 2 Kings 15:7.

verses.text: Jotham took the throne at age twenty-five and reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. Jerushah, Zadok’s daughter, was his mother.{a}
Following Uzziah’s good example, Jotham did right in Yahweh’s eyes. Yet he never copied his father’s sin of entering Yahweh’s temple to burn incense. Still, the people kept on doing wrong.{b}
Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of Yahweh’s temple. He also did a great deal of building on the wall at Ophel.{c}
He built towns in Judah’s hill country, and he put up forts and towers in the wooded areas.

He fought the king of the Ammonites and beat them. That year the Ammonites paid him about three and three-quarter tons of silver, sixty thousand bushels of wheat and sixty thousand bushels of barley. Year two and year three, they paid that much again.{d}
Jotham grew powerful, because he was careful to live in a way that pleased Yahweh his God.
Everything else about Jotham, all his wars and the things he did, is recorded in the book about the kings of Israel and Judah.
He had been twenty-five when he became king, and his reign in Jerusalem lasted sixteen years.
Jotham died and joined his forefathers, and they buried him in David’s City. Ahaz, his son, followed him as king.{e}

notes.text: Jerushah means “owned.” Zadok means “right” or “fair.” Chapter 27 is much like 2 Kings 15:32-38.
This means he did not dare to burn incense as Uzziah had done (26:16).
Ophel means “hill” or “swelling.” It was the strong ridge just south of the temple.
The Hebrew says “a hundred talents” of silver and “ten thousand cors” each of wheat and barley. A talent weighed about 75 pounds, and a cor held about six bushels.
Ahaz means “he has taken hold.”

verses.text: Ahaz became king when he was twenty years old. He reigned from Jerusalem for sixteen years. Unlike his forefather David, he did not do what was right in Yahweh’s eyes.{a}
Instead he copied the kings of Israel. He even cast metal idols of the Baal gods.
He burned incense in Ben-hinnom Valley, and he burned his own sons as sacrifices. He copied the disgusting practices of the nations Yahweh had driven out ahead of the Israelites.{b}
On hilltops, on hills of every kind and beneath each spreading green tree, he made sacrifices and sent up incense smoke.

Because of this, Yahweh his God put Ahaz at the mercy of Aram’s king. The Arameans beat him and took a large number of his people away as prisoners to Damascus. Yahweh also let Israel’s king defeat Ahaz, and many of his people were slaughtered.{c}
In a single day, Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 brave soldiers in Judah. It happened because Judah had abandoned Yahweh, the God their forefathers served.{d}
Zichri, a warrior from Ephraim, killed three men close to Ahaz: Maaseiah, the king’s son; Azrikam, who ran the palace; and Elkanah, the king’s second-in-command.{e}
Israel’s soldiers captured 200,000 of their own relatives from Judah, women and children included. They also took huge amounts of loot and brought it back to Samaria.

But a prophet of Yahweh named Oded lived there. He went out to meet the army as it came back to Samaria. “Listen!” he told them. “Yahweh, the God of your forefathers, was angry with Judah. That is why he let you defeat them. But you killed them with such fury that it has reached all the way to heaven.{f}
Now you intend to force Jerusalem’s and Judah’s people into slavery, men and women alike. But aren’t you guilty of sins against Yahweh your God too?
So listen to me! Send these prisoners home. They are your own relatives. Yahweh’s fierce anger is hanging over you.”

Then some of the leaders of Ephraim stood up against the soldiers coming home from the war. Among them were Amasa, whose father was Hadlai; Jehizkiah, whose father was Shallum; Berechiah, whose father was Meshillemoth; and Azariah, whose father was Johanan.{g}

“Don’t bring these captives in here!” they said. “Yahweh would count it as a sin against us. You want to pile more on top of all our sins and guilt. We are already very guilty, and God’s fierce anger is aimed at Israel.”
So with the leaders and the whole assembly watching, the soldiers let go of the captives and handed over the loot.

Then those four leaders, named above, took charge of the prisoners. Some of them had nothing to wear, so the leaders dressed them from the loot. They handed out clothing, sandals, meals and water, and oil to soothe their skin. They put the weak ones on donkeys. Then they led them all to Jericho, the palm tree city, and handed them back to their own people. After that, they returned to Samaria.{h}
About this time, King Ahaz sent to Assyria’s king asking for help.{i}
The Edomites had invaded Judah again, attacking the people and carrying off prisoners.

The Philistines had also raided the towns in Judah’s western hills and in the Negev, the dry land in the south. They captured Beth-shemesh, Aijalon and Gederoth. They took Soco, Timnah and Gimzo with their villages, and they moved in to live there.{j}
Yahweh was humbling Judah because of Ahaz, Israel’s king. Ahaz had let Judah run wild, and he had been terribly unfaithful to Yahweh.{k}
Tilgath-pilneser, Assyria’s king, did come to him. But instead of helping Ahaz, he caused him trouble.{l}
Ahaz took some of the treasures from Yahweh’s temple, from the palace and from the officials’ homes. He gave them to Assyria’s king, but it did him no good.{m}
During this time of trouble, King Ahaz grew even more unfaithful to Yahweh.

He sacrificed to Damascus’s gods, though Damascus had beaten him. He thought, “The gods of Aram’s kings helped them. So I will offer sacrifices to them, and maybe they will help me.” Instead they brought ruin on him and on all Israel.{n}
Ahaz collected the objects used in God’s temple and smashed them. He locked up the doors of Yahweh’s house. Then he set up altars for himself on every street corner in Jerusalem.{o}
In each town of Judah he built hilltop shrines for burning incense to other gods. This made Yahweh, his forefathers’ God, very angry.
For the rest of his story and all his ways, from start to finish, see the book of Judah’s and Israel’s kings.
Ahaz died and joined his forefathers. They buried him inside the city of Jerusalem, but they did not bring him into the tombs of Israel’s kings. Hezekiah, his son, took over as king.{p}

notes.text: For Ahaz, see 27:9. Verses 1-4 are much like 2 Kings 16:1-4. It is very hard to make his age fit with his son Hezekiah’s age (29:1). See 2 Kings 16:2 and 18:2.
The meaning of Hinnom is not known. This valley was just south of Jerusalem, and later it was called Gehenna. 2 Kings 16:3 says “made his son pass through the fire.”
See 2 Kings 16:5-6 and Isaiah 7:1-9. They tell about Aram and Israel attacking together, but they do not mention a lost battle.
Pekah means “open (eyes).” Remaliah may mean “Yahweh has decorated.” Verses 6-15 are not in Kings. For the large numbers, see the note at 13:3.
For Zichri, see 17:16. For Maaseiah, see 23:1. Azrikam means “my help has risen.” Elkanah means “God has made” or “God has gained.”
For Oded, see 15:1.

For Azariah, see 15:1. Johanan means “Yahweh is kind.” Berechiah means “Yahweh blesses.” Meshillemoth means “payback.” Jehizkiah means “Yahweh makes strong,” another form of Hezekiah. Shallum means “payback.” Amasa means “load.” Hadlai means “resting.”
Jericho may mean “moon city” or “sweet-smelling.” See Luke 10:30-37.
The Hebrew says “kings.” The Greek translation says “king.” 2 Kings 16:7 names him as Tiglath-pileser.
Negev means “south” or “dry land.” Aijalon means “place of deer.” Gederoth means “walls” or “sheep pens.” Soco means “thorny.” Timnah means “share.” Gimzo may mean “place of fig trees.”
“King of Israel” here means king of Judah (see the note at 21:2). The Greek translation says “king of Judah.”

Tilgath-pilneser is how Chronicles spells Tiglath-pileser the Third, king of Assyria from about 745 to 727 BC. His name means “my trust is in the son of Esharra.” 2 Kings 16:9 says he did help Ahaz by capturing Damascus. Chronicles points out that this help did Judah no lasting good.
See 2 Kings 16:8, 17-18.
2 Kings 16:10-16 says Ahaz copied an altar he saw in Damascus.
2 Kings 16:17-18 tells how he took away parts of the temple. Only Chronicles says he shut the temple doors (see 29:3, 7).
2 Kings 16:20 says Ahaz was buried with his forefathers in David’s City. Hezekiah means “Yahweh makes strong.”

verses.text: Hezekiah came to the throne at twenty-five. He reigned twenty-nine years from Jerusalem. Abijah, Zechariah’s daughter, was his mother.{a}
He did right in Yahweh’s eyes, following the full example of his forefather David.
In the very first month of his first year as king, in March or April, Hezekiah unlocked the doors of Yahweh’s temple and repaired them.{b}
He called in the priests and Levites and met with them in the open square on the east side.
“Levites, listen to me!” he said. “Make yourselves holy now. Then make holy the temple of Yahweh, the God your forefathers served. Clear every filthy thing out of the holy place.{c}
Our fathers broke faith. In the eyes of Yahweh our God they did wrong, and they walked away from him. They looked away from his home and showed it their backs.
They closed up the porch doors and let the lamps go out. They stopped burning incense in the holy place, and they stopped bringing burnt offerings to Israel’s God.
That is why Yahweh’s anger came down on Judah and Jerusalem. He made them a thing of horror and shock, something people hiss at. You are witnesses of all this.{d}
It is the reason our fathers fell by the sword, and the reason our wives and children are prisoners in foreign lands.
So I have decided to make a covenant with Yahweh, Israel’s God, hoping his blazing anger will leave us.
My sons, don’t be lazy now. You are the ones Yahweh picked to come before him as his servants. You are to lead his worship and burn incense to him.”

So the Levites got to work. Among the Kohathites, Mahath, Amasai’s son, and Joel, Azariah’s son, stepped forward. Among the Merarites, Kish, Abdi’s son, and Azariah, Jehallelel’s son, did the same. Among the Gershonites, it was Joah, Zimmah’s son, and Eden, Joah’s son.{e}
From Elizaphan’s family came Shimri and Jeiel. From Asaph’s family came Zechariah and Mattaniah.{f}
From Heman’s family came Jehiel and Shimei. From Jeduthun’s family came Shemaiah and Uzziel.{g}
These men gathered their fellow Levites, and they all made themselves holy. Then they went in to clean Yahweh’s temple, as the king had ordered. They were following Yahweh’s own words.

The priests went into the inner part of Yahweh’s temple to clean it. They carried out into the temple courtyard every unclean thing they found in there. Then the Levites hauled it all away to the Kidron Valley.

They started the work of purifying on the first of the first month. By the eighth day they had reached Yahweh’s porch. They spent eight more days making the temple holy. On the sixteenth day of the first month, they finished.{h}

Then they went to see King Hezekiah in the palace. “We have cleaned all of Yahweh’s temple,” they reported. “We cleaned the altar for burnt offerings and all its tools. We cleaned the table for the holy bread and everything used with it.
When King Ahaz was unfaithful during his reign, he threw out many of the temple objects. We have gotten all of them ready again and made them holy. They are now in front of Yahweh’s altar.”
Early the next morning, King Hezekiah gathered the city’s officials and went up to Yahweh’s temple.

They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs and seven male goats as a sin offering. These were to cover the kingdom, the holy place and Judah’s people. Hezekiah ordered Aaron’s descendants, the priests, to sacrifice them on Yahweh’s altar.

So the bulls were killed, and the priests caught the blood and splashed it on the altar. Then the rams were killed, and their blood was splashed on the altar. Then the lambs were killed, and their blood was splashed on the altar too.
Last, the male goats for the sin offering were led up in front of Hezekiah and the crowd. They placed their hands on the goats.

The priests killed the goats and put their blood on the altar as a sin offering. This was to make all Israel right with God. The king had ordered the burnt offering and the sin offering to be given for all Israel.{i}

Hezekiah placed Levites in Yahweh’s temple with cymbals, harps and lyres. This was what David had commanded, and what Gad, the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet had commanded. The command really came from Yahweh, through his prophets.{j}
The Levites stood ready with the instruments David had made. The priests stood ready with the trumpets.
Hezekiah now commanded that the altar fire receive the burnt offering. At that moment the song to Yahweh started up as well. Trumpets played, along with the instruments of David, Israel’s king.
All the people bowed down in worship. The singers sang and the trumpeters played the whole time, until the burnt offering was finished.
Once the sacrificing was over, the king and all those around him bowed low and worshiped.
Next, the king and his officials directed the Levites to praise Yahweh using the words of David and of Asaph the seer. So they sang praises with great joy. Then they bowed down and worshiped.

Hezekiah spoke up: “Now that you have set yourselves apart for Yahweh, come forward. Bring sacrifices and thank offerings to Yahweh’s temple.” The crowd did just that, and those whose hearts moved them added burnt offerings as well.{k}
For burnt offerings to Yahweh the crowd gave two hundred lambs, a hundred rams, and seventy bulls.
They also gave six hundred cattle and three thousand sheep and goats as holy gifts.

But the priests were too few to strip the hides from so many animals. Their Levite relatives pitched in until the job was finished and until more priests were ready. The Levites had shown more care about purifying themselves than the priests had.
Burnt offerings were plentiful, and with them came the fat of the peace offerings and the drink offerings that went with each burnt offering. And so the service in Yahweh’s temple was set up again.
Hezekiah and all the people were full of joy at what God had done for his people, because it had all happened so quickly.

notes.text: For Hezekiah, see 28:27. Abijah means “Yahweh is my father.” 2 Kings 18:2 calls her Abi. For Zechariah, see 17:7. See 2 Kings 18:1-3. Most of chapters 29-31 is not in Kings.
This was the month later called Nisan, the first month of the year counting from spring.
Or “the uncleanness,” meaning anything that made the temple unclean, such as idols or the things used to worship them.
Hebrew copies spell the word for “horror” in two slightly different ways. See Jeremiah 29:18.

Mahath means “grabbing.” Amasai means “load carrier.” Joel means “Yahweh is God.” For Azariah, see 15:1. For the Kohathites, see 20:19. Merari means “bitter.” Kish may mean “bow.” Abdi means “my servant.” Jehallelel means “he praises God.” The Gershonites came from Gershon, which means “driven out” or “foreigner.” Joah means “Yahweh is brother.” Zimmah means “plan.” Eden means “delight.”
Elizaphan means “God has hidden.” Shimri means “my guard.” For Jeiel, Asaph and Mattaniah, see 20:14.
Heman means “faithful.” For Jehiel, see 21:2. Shimei means “heard.” Jeduthun may mean “praise.” For Shemaiah, see 11:2. Uzziel means “God is my strength.”
The sixteenth day was after the date set for Passover, the fourteenth day of the first month. That is why Passover was held in the second month (30:2).
“All Israel” includes the northern tribes (see 30:1).
Gad means “good luck.” Nathan means “he has given.” See 1 Chronicles 23-25.
The Hebrew says “Now you have filled your hand,” a way of saying “you have been ordained.”

subheads.18: The Temple Is Made Holy Again

verses.text: Hezekiah sent word to every part of Israel and Judah. Letters went out from him to Ephraim and Manasseh as well, calling everyone to come to Yahweh’s temple in Jerusalem and celebrate the Passover for Yahweh, Israel’s God.{a}
The king, his officials and the whole gathering in Jerusalem had talked it over. They agreed to hold the Passover in the second month, in April or May.{b}
They could not hold it at the usual time. Not enough priests had made themselves holy yet, and the people had not had time to gather in Jerusalem.
Hezekiah liked the plan, and so did the whole assembly.

So they decided to send out a message all over Israel, from Beersheba up to Dan. It told everyone to come to Jerusalem and keep Yahweh’s Passover. Most people had not been keeping it in the way the Law describes.{c}

Runners carried letters from the king and his officials through all of Israel and Judah. The king’s message said: “People of Israel, come back to Yahweh, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel! Then he will come back to you who are left, you who got away from the kings of Assyria.{d}
Don’t act like your fathers and your relatives. They were unfaithful to Yahweh, the God their forefathers served. So he made them a wasteland, as you can see.
Don’t be stubborn like your fathers were. Give yourselves to Yahweh. Come to his temple, which he has made holy forever. Serve Yahweh your God, and his fierce rage against you will cool.{e}

Turn to Yahweh again, and your captured relatives and children will find mercy from their captors. They will let them come home to this land. Yahweh your God is kind and full of mercy. If you return to him, he will not look away from you.”
Through Ephraim’s and Manasseh’s land the runners hurried, town after town, as far as Zebulun. People there only laughed and jeered at them.{f}
Still, some men from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun were humble enough to come to Jerusalem.{g}
In Judah, too, God was at work. He made the people united in their desire to obey what the king and his officials ordered, as Yahweh had said.
A huge crowd of people came to Jerusalem in the second month, in April or May, to celebrate the Festival of Bread Without Yeast.
They set to work and removed the altars in Jerusalem. Every incense altar was hauled off and thrown into Kidron’s ravine.

On the fourteenth of the second month, the Passover lambs were slaughtered. The priests and Levites felt ashamed, so they made themselves holy. Then they brought burnt offerings to Yahweh’s temple.{h}
Each stood at his assigned post, following the Law of Moses, God’s prophet. The Levites handed the blood to the priests, and the priests splashed it on the altar.
A good part of the crowd had not been purified. So the Levites were put in charge of killing the Passover lambs for everyone who was unclean. That way the lambs could be set apart for Yahweh.

Large numbers of the people, especially from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun, had not made themselves clean. Even so, they ate the Passover, though this was not what the Law says. But Hezekiah prayed for them. “Yahweh is good,” he said. “May he forgive everyone{i}
who has set his heart on seeking God, on Yahweh, the God his forefathers served. Forgive them even if they are not clean by the rules of the holy place.”
Yahweh heard Hezekiah’s prayer, and he healed the people.

For seven days the Israelites gathered in Jerusalem kept the Festival of Bread Without Yeast. They were filled with joy. Every day the Levites and priests praised Yahweh, singing to him with loud instruments.{j}

Hezekiah spoke warm words of thanks to all the Levites who showed great skill in serving Yahweh. For the seven days of the festival, the people ate their share of the food. They offered peace offerings and gave praise to Yahweh, the God their forefathers served.{k}
Then the whole crowd agreed to keep the festival going for seven more days. Their happy celebration went on for a second week.

Hezekiah, Judah’s king, provided a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep for the people’s offerings. His officials added a thousand more bulls and ten thousand sheep. By this time a large number of priests had made themselves holy.
Everyone was full of joy: the people of Judah, the priests and Levites, all those who came from Israel, and the foreigners who had come from Israel or who lived in Judah.
Jerusalem was filled with joy. The city had seen no celebration like it since the time of Solomon, David’s son, who was king of Israel.
Then the Levite priests stood up and blessed the people. God heard them. Their prayer reached heaven, the holy place where he lives.

notes.text: For Ephraim, see 13:4. For Manasseh, see 15:9. The Hebrew word for Passover is pesah.
This was the month later called Iyyar, the second month counting from spring. Numbers 9:6-13 allows a Passover in the second month for people who are unclean or far away.
Dan means “judge.” Or “for they had not kept it for a long time as the Law says.”
Abraham means “father of many.” Isaac means “he laughs.” Israel means “he struggles with God.” The northern kingdom had already fallen to Assyria (2 Kings 17).
The Hebrew says “give the hand to Yahweh,” a sign of giving in to him.
Zebulun means “home” or “honor.”
Asher means “happy.”
Passover was normally on the fourteenth day of the first month (Exodus 12:6). See the note at verse 2.
Issachar means “there is a reward.” The Greek translation joins “saying” to verse 19.

The Festival of Bread Without Yeast ran from the fifteenth to the twenty-first of the month. The Hebrew says “with instruments of strength.” Some read “with all their strength” (see 1 Chronicles 13:8).
Or “spoke kindly to.” Or “giving thanks to Yahweh.”

verses.text: When the festival was over, the Israelites who had come went out into the towns of Judah. They smashed the sacred stone pillars and chopped down the Asherah poles. They pulled down the hilltop shrines and the altars all over Judah and Benjamin, and in Ephraim and Manasseh too, until nothing was left of them. After that, every Israelite went home to his own town and land.

Hezekiah set up the work groups of priests and Levites again. Each man had his own task. Some offered the burnt offerings and the peace offerings. Others served, gave thanks, and sang praise at the gates of Yahweh’s camp.{a}

From his own herds and flocks, the king gave animals for the burnt offerings. These were for the morning and evening offerings, for Sabbath days, for each new moon, and for the yearly festivals, just as Yahweh’s Law required.
He also told the people living in Jerusalem to bring the share that belonged to the priests and Levites. Then those men would be free to give all their time to Yahweh’s Law.

The order spread, and right away the Israelites gave with open hands. They carried in grain, new wine, olive oil, and honey from the first of their harvest, along with everything else their fields grew. A tenth of all they had was brought, and the amount was enormous.

Judah’s towns had people from both Israel and Judah living in them. They, too, gave a tenth of their cattle and sheep, plus a tenth of the holy things set apart for Yahweh their God. All of it they stacked into heaps.
They started making the piles in the third month (in May–June). They finished in the seventh month (in September–October).{b}
When the king and his officials came to look at the heaps, they gave praise to Yahweh. They spoke blessings on Israel, his people.
Then Hezekiah wanted to know from the priests and Levites why the heaps were there.

Azariah the head priest, from Zadok’s family, gave the answer. “Ever since the people started bringing their gifts to Yahweh’s temple,” he said, “we have had plenty to eat, with lots left over. Yahweh has blessed his people. That is why so much is still here.”{c}
So Hezekiah ordered storerooms to be made ready in Yahweh’s temple, and the work was done.
The people faithfully carried in the gifts, the tenths, and the holy things. Conaniah the Levite was put in charge of all of it, and his brother Shimei was next under him.{d}

Under Conaniah and Shimei his brother, ten men served as supervisors: Jehiel and Azaziah, Nahath and Asahel, Jerimoth and Jozabad, Eliel and Ismachiah, Mahath and Benaiah. King Hezekiah had picked them, together with Azariah, the man in charge of God’s temple.{e}

The East Gate was kept by Kore, a Levite whose father was Imnah. He took care of the gifts people chose to give God. It was his job to hand out what was offered to Yahweh, and the most holy gifts as well.{f}

Helping him in the priests’ towns were Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah. They were trusted to share the food fairly with the other priests by their work groups, the old and the young alike.{g}
They also gave to the males listed in the family records who were three years old or older. This covered everyone who came into Yahweh’s temple to do his daily work by his group and duty.{h}
The priests were listed by their family lines. The Levites twenty years old and older were listed by their duties and groups.
The records included all the little children, the wives, the sons, and the daughters of the whole community. The workers were faithful in keeping themselves holy for this task.

Some of Aaron’s descendants, the priests, lived on the farm land around their towns. In each of those towns, men were named to hand out shares to every male priest and to every Levite listed in the records.
This is how Hezekiah acted all through Judah. He did what was good and right and true in the eyes of Yahweh his God.
Everything he started for the service of God’s temple, and everything he did to obey God’s Law and commands, he did with all his heart to seek his God. And it all went well for him.

notes.text: “Yahweh’s camp” means the temple area. The name recalls Israel’s camp in the desert.
The third month was later called Sivan, the time of the grain harvest. The seventh month was later called Tishri, the time of the fruit harvest.
Zadok means “right” or “fair.”
Conaniah means “Yahweh has made firm.”
Azaziah means “Yahweh is strong.” Nahath means “rest.” Jozabad means “Yahweh has given.” Ismachiah means “Yahweh holds up.”
Kore means “one who calls” or “partridge.” Imnah means “good luck.”
Miniamin means “from the right hand.” Jeshua means “Yahweh saves.” Shecaniah means “Yahweh lives here.”
The Hebrew says “three years.” Some think it should be “thirty years” (see 1 Chronicles 23:3), but it may mean the families who were fed.

verses.text: Hezekiah had served God faithfully. After all of that, Sennacherib, Assyria’s king, marched into Judah. He camped outside its walled towns, planning to break in and take them for himself.{a}
Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had arrived and meant to attack Jerusalem.
He met with his officials and his best fighters to plan. Together they decided to stop up the springs outside the city so no water flowed from them. The men helped him with this.
A big crowd came together. They stopped up all the springs and the stream that ran through the land. “Why let Assyria’s kings come here and find plenty of water?” they asked.{b}

Hezekiah worked hard to make the city strong. He repaired every broken part of the wall and built towers on it. Outside it he built a second wall. He made the Millo in David’s City stronger, too, and he had large numbers of spears and shields made.{c}
He put army officers over the people. Then he called them together in the open square by the city gate. He spoke to them to encourage them.
“Be strong and brave!” he said. “Don’t let the king of Assyria or his huge army scare you or make you lose heart. The One on our side is greater than anyone on his side.{d}
The Assyrian has nothing but the strength of men. On our side stands Yahweh our God. He will help us, and he will do our fighting!” The people trusted these words from Hezekiah, Judah’s king.

Later Sennacherib, Assyria’s king, was attacking Lachish with all his troops. From there he sent officers to Jerusalem with a message for Hezekiah, Judah’s king, and for all the Judeans in the city.{e}
They brought word from Sennacherib, king of Assyria: ‘What are you relying on, that you sit tight in Jerusalem while my army surrounds it?
Hezekiah is leading you astray! He tells you that Yahweh your God will snatch you out of my hands. All he is doing is getting you ready to die of hunger and thirst.
Wasn’t it this same Hezekiah who got rid of Yahweh’s hilltop shrines and altars? He told Judah and Jerusalem, “You must worship at just one altar and burn incense on it alone.”{f}
You have heard what I and the kings before me did to nation after nation. Did their gods have the power to save their countries from my hand? No!
My ancestors wiped out those nations. Not one of their gods could save its people from me. So how could your God save you from me?

So do not let Hezekiah fool you. Do not let him talk you into this. Do not trust him! Never has a god of any people or kingdom rescued its nation from me or the kings before me. Your God will surely fail as well!’”
The king’s officers said even more against Yahweh God and against Hezekiah, who served him.

Sennacherib sent letters as well, letters that made fun of Yahweh, the God of Israel. They said, “Other lands had gods, but those gods could not rescue their people from my hand. Hezekiah’s God won’t rescue his people from me either.”
The officers shouted in the Judeans’ own language to the people standing on Jerusalem’s wall. They wanted to frighten them and make them panic so the city would be easy to capture.
The officers spoke of Jerusalem’s God the same way they spoke of the gods of the world’s other peoples, which are only things that human hands have made.
King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz cried out to heaven in prayer about this.{g}

So Yahweh sent an angel. The angel wiped out every brave soldier, commander, and officer in Assyria’s camp. Sennacherib went back to his own country with his face covered in shame. Later, while he was in the temple of his god, sons who were his own children struck him down with the sword.{h}
In this way Yahweh rescued Hezekiah and the people living in Jerusalem from Sennacherib, Assyria’s king, and from all their enemies. He guarded them on all sides.{i}
People came to Jerusalem carrying gifts for Yahweh, and many brought valuable presents for Hezekiah, Judah’s king. After that, every nation looked up to him.
About then Hezekiah fell sick and came close to death. He prayed to Yahweh, who spoke to him and gave him a sign of wonder.{j}
But Hezekiah grew proud and did not show thanks for the kindness he had been shown. So God was angry with him and with Judah and Jerusalem.
Then Hezekiah stopped being proud and humbled himself, and so did the people of Jerusalem. Because of that, Yahweh’s anger did not fall on them while Hezekiah was alive.
Hezekiah became very rich and greatly honored. He made treasure rooms to hold his silver and gold, his jewels and spices, his shields, and all sorts of valuable things.
He built storehouses for the grain, new wine, and olive oil his land produced. He made stalls for all kinds of cattle and pens for his flocks.{k}
He built towns for himself, and he owned huge numbers of sheep and cattle. God had made him extremely rich.
Hezekiah is the king who closed off the upper opening where the Gihon spring flowed out. He made the water run down to the west side of David’s City. Everything Hezekiah did went well.{l}

Once, though, the rulers of Babylon sent messengers to ask him about the amazing sign that had happened in the land. At that time God left Hezekiah alone to test him. God did this so that all that was in his heart would come out.{m}
More about Hezekiah’s rule and the good he did can be found in writing. It is in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, part of the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.

Hezekiah died and joined his ancestors. They buried him high on the slope with the graves of David’s family. When he died, the whole of Judah and all Jerusalem’s people gave him honor. Manasseh, his son, then ruled in his place.{n}

notes.text: Sennacherib means “the god Sin has replaced the brothers.” He was king of Assyria about 705-681 BC and invaded Judah in 701 BC. This chapter is a shorter form of 2 Kings 18:13-20:21 (see Isaiah 36-39).
The Septuagint says “the king of Assyria.”
Millo means “filling.” It was probably a raised earth platform or fortress (see 1 Chronicles 11:8).
See 2 Kings 6:16.
For Lachish, see 25:27.
Sennacherib thought Hezekiah’s changes (31:1) had made Yahweh angry. See 2 Kings 18:22.
For Isaiah, see 26:22. See 2 Kings 19:14-19.
Second Kings 19:35 says 185,000 soldiers died. Sennacherib was killed in 681 BC, about twenty years later (2 Kings 19:37).
The Hebrew says “he guided them.” The Septuagint says “he gave them rest.”
See 2 Kings 20:1-11 and Isaiah 38. There the sign was a shadow moving back on the steps.
The Hebrew may also mean “folds for flocks.”
Gihon means “gushing.” This is the tunnel now called Hezekiah’s Tunnel, about 1,750 feet (533 meters) long. See 2 Kings 20:20.
See 2 Kings 20:12-19 and Isaiah 39. The sign was the one in verse 24.
Or “in the upper part of the tombs.”

verses.text: At age twelve Manasseh took the throne. His rule from Jerusalem lasted fifty-five years.{a}
Yahweh saw Manasseh doing evil. He copied the disgusting practices of the nations that Yahweh had driven out to make room for the Israelites.

The hilltop shrines that his father Hezekiah had pulled down, Manasseh built back up. He put up altars to the Baal gods and made Asherah poles. The whole army of stars overhead became his gods; he knelt to them and gave them his service.
He even built altars inside Yahweh’s temple. Yet Yahweh had said of that place, “Jerusalem is where my Name will stay forever.”
In both courtyards of Yahweh’s temple he built altars to honor the stars.

In Hinnom’s Son Valley he burned his own sons as offerings. He used magic, looked for signs to tell the future, and practiced witchcraft. He went to people who talked with the spirits of the dead, and to fortune-tellers. Again and again he did what Yahweh saw as evil, and he made Yahweh angry.{b}

Manasseh carved an idol and set it up inside God’s temple. That was the very place God had spoken of to David and his son Solomon. God had said, “Out of all Israel’s tribes I chose Jerusalem. My Name will stay in this temple, in that city, forever.{c}

Israel’s feet will not be forced off the land I gave their ancestors ever again, if only they will be careful to obey me. They must do everything I commanded them in all the teachings, rules, and laws I gave through Moses.”
But Manasseh led Judah and Jerusalem’s people off the right path. They did worse evil than the nations Yahweh had wiped out ahead of the Israelites.
Yahweh warned Manasseh and the people, yet they paid no attention.
So Yahweh sent the army commanders of Assyria’s king to attack them. They caught Manasseh, put hooks in him, chained him with bronze chains, and dragged him off to Babylon.{d}
In his trouble Manasseh begged Yahweh his God for mercy. He made himself very low before the God of his ancestors.
When he prayed, God was moved by his begging and listened to his cry. He brought him home to Jerusalem and gave him back his kingdom. Then Manasseh knew for certain that Yahweh is God.{e}

Afterward Manasseh built a high outer wall for David’s City. Starting in the valley on the western side of Gihon spring, it stretched to the entrance by the Fish Gate and went around Ophel hill. He made it very tall. In every walled town of Judah he stationed army commanders.{f}
He cleared the foreign gods out of Yahweh’s temple, along with the idol. On the temple hill and in Jerusalem he had built altars. He took them all down and threw them outside the city.
He rebuilt Yahweh’s altar and offered peace offerings and thank offerings on it. He gave Judah orders to serve Yahweh, Israel’s God.{g}
The people kept making sacrifices at the hilltop shrines, but now only to Yahweh their God.
More about Manasseh is written in the records of Israel’s kings. That includes his prayer to his God and the messages the seers gave him in the name of Yahweh, Israel’s God.{h}

The records of Hozai tell about his prayer and how God answered his plea. They tell of all his sins and unfaithfulness. They list the places where he built hilltop shrines and set up Asherah poles and idols before he humbled himself.{i}
Manasseh died and joined his ancestors, and he was buried at his palace. His son Amon became the next king.{j}
Amon took the throne when he was twenty-two. He ruled from Jerusalem for two years.{k}
Amon did evil in Yahweh’s eyes, as his father Manasseh had. Every carved image Manasseh had made received sacrifices and worship from Amon.
His father Manasseh had humbled himself before Yahweh, but Amon never did. Instead, he kept piling up more and more guilt.
Amon’s own officials made a secret plan against him and killed him inside his palace.
Then the people of the land put to death all who had plotted against King Amon. They made Josiah, his son, king to take his place.{l}

notes.text: Verses 1-10 are much like 2 Kings 21:1-10. Verses 18-25 are much like 2 Kings 21:17-24.
The Hebrew says “made his sons pass through the fire.” Second Kings 21:6 says “his son.” See Deuteronomy 18:10-11.
Second Kings 21:7 says it was an idol of Asherah.

Or “with nose hooks.” Old Assyrian carvings show prisoners led this way. Kings does not tell about Manasseh being taken away and turning back (verses 11-17). At that time Babylon was ruled by Assyria.
A later Jewish writing called the Prayer of Manasseh says it is this prayer. It is found in some Greek Bibles.
For Gihon, see 32:30. For Ophel, see 27:3.
Some Hebrew copies say “he prepared.” Others say “he built.”
The Hebrew says “the words of the kings of Israel,” meaning their records.
Hozai means “my seers.” The Septuagint says “the seers.”
Second Kings 21:18 says he was buried in his palace garden, the garden of Uzza.
See 2 Kings 21:19-26.
Josiah means “Yahweh holds up” or “Yahweh heals.”

verses.text: Josiah was only eight when he was crowned. From Jerusalem he ruled thirty-one years.{a}
Josiah did right in Yahweh’s eyes. He lived the way his ancestor David had lived, and he kept to that path without turning aside either way.

In the eighth year he was king, while still a boy, Josiah started to seek the God of his ancestor David. By his twelfth year he began to clean up Judah and Jerusalem. He removed the hilltop shrines, the Asherah poles, the carved idols, and the metal statues.{b}

While Josiah watched, his men broke apart the Baal altars. He chopped down the incense altars that stood over them. He smashed the Asherah poles and every idol, carved or cast, and beat them into dust. That dust he sprinkled on the tombs of those who had once offered sacrifices to these idols.{c}
The priests of those idols were long dead, but Josiah had their bones burned on the very altars where they had served. So he cleansed Judah and Jerusalem.{d}
Manasseh’s towns, Ephraim’s, and Simeon’s got the same treatment, and so did towns all the way to Naphtali, in the ruins all around them.{e}
All over the land of Israel he tore down altars and crushed Asherah poles and idols to powder. He cut down every incense altar. After that he came back to Jerusalem.

In Josiah’s eighteenth year, once the land and the temple were clean, he sent three men to fix up the temple of Yahweh his God. They were Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the city’s governor, and Joah son of Joahaz, who kept the royal records.{f}

They went to Hilkiah the high priest. They handed him the money that had come into God’s temple. The Levites who guarded the doors had collected it from the people of Manasseh and Ephraim, from everyone left in Israel, from all Judah and Benjamin, and from those who lived in Jerusalem.{g}
Then they gave the money to the men in charge of the work on Yahweh’s temple. Those men paid the workers who were fixing and restoring it.
They paid the carpenters and builders, who bought cut stone and wood. The wood was for braces and beams in the buildings that Judah’s kings had let fall apart.

The workers were honest and faithful. Levites led the work and kept it moving. Two came from Merari’s family, Jahath and Obadiah. Two came from Kohath’s family, Zechariah and Meshullam. Other Levites, all skilled musicians,
were in charge of the men who carried loads, and they directed every worker at every job. Some Levites served as writers, some as officials, and some as gatekeepers.{h}
They were taking out the money brought into Yahweh’s temple, when Hilkiah the priest came upon a book. It was the book of Yahweh’s Law that had been given through Moses.{i}
Hilkiah told Shaphan the royal secretary, “In Yahweh’s temple I have found the Law book!” He put the book into Shaphan’s hands.
Shaphan brought it to the king. He also reported, “Your officials are carrying out all the jobs you gave them.
They emptied out the money that was in Yahweh’s temple. Now the supervisors and workmen have it.”
Then Shaphan the secretary added, “Hilkiah the priest gave me a book.” And he read from it to the king.
As the king listened to the words of the Law, he ripped his robes in grief.
The king then commanded five men: Hilkiah; Ahikam, whose father was Shaphan; Abdon, whose father was Micah; Shaphan, the secretary; and Asaiah, who served the king.{j}

“Go and ask Yahweh what this means,” he said. “Ask on my behalf, and on behalf of those still left of Israel and Judah. Ask about what is written in this book we found. Yahweh’s anger is pouring down on us like a flood. Our ancestors did not keep Yahweh’s word. They failed to do what this book says.”

So Hilkiah and the others the king had sent went to see Huldah, a woman prophet. She lived in Jerusalem’s Second District. Her husband was Shallum, who looked after the royal clothes. He was the son of Tokhath and grandson of Hasrah. They told her what had happened.{k}
Huldah said to them, “Yahweh, Israel’s God, has this to say. Give this message to the man who sent you here:
‘Yahweh says, Look, disaster is coming from me. It will strike this place and all who live in it. Every curse written in the book read aloud to Judah’s king will happen.
They walked away from me and burned incense to other gods. Everything they have made has stirred up my anger. So my anger will pour out on this place, and no one will be able to put it out.’{l}
Judah’s king sent you to ask Yahweh what to do. Tell him, ‘Yahweh, Israel’s God, speaks to you about the words you heard.
