When you heard what I said against this place and its people, your heart was soft. You humbled yourself in front of God. You bowed low before me, tore your robes, and cried in my presence. So I have heard you, says Yahweh.

I will let you die and join your ancestors. When you go to your grave, it will be in peace. You will not live to see the disaster I am bringing on this place and its people.’” The men went back and told the king her answer.{m}
Then the king called for all the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem to meet together.

He went up to Yahweh’s temple. With him went everyone from Judah and Jerusalem, priests and Levites too, the great and the small alike. There, while they listened, he read out the whole book of the agreement that had been found in Yahweh’s temple.

The king stood at his place. In Yahweh’s presence he made a solemn agreement to follow Yahweh. He promised to obey his commands, his warnings, and his rules with all his heart and soul. He would carry out everything written in this book.{n}
He had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin promise to keep the agreement too. So Jerusalem’s people lived by the agreement they had made with God, whom their ancestors had served.

Josiah removed every disgusting idol from all the lands that belonged to the Israelites. He made everyone in Israel worship Yahweh their God. As long as Josiah lived, they did not stop following Yahweh, the God of their ancestors.

notes.text: Chapters 34-35 are much like 2 Kings 22:1-23:30. But Chronicles tells about removing the idols (verses 3-7) before the book was found. Kings tells it after (2 Kings 23:4-20).
In the eighth year Josiah was about sixteen. The twelfth year was about 628 BC.
These were incense altars or sun pillars (see 14:5).
See 1 Kings 13:2 and 2 Kings 23:16, 20.
The Hebrew here is hard to understand. The meaning is not certain.
Shaphan means “rock badger.” Azaliah means “Yahweh has kept back.” Joahaz means “Yahweh has taken hold.” The eighteenth year was about 622 BC.
Hilkiah means “Yahweh is my share.” Some Hebrew copies say “they went back to Jerusalem.”
Verses 12-13 can also be divided differently. Jahath may mean “he will snatch up.” Meshullam means “paid back” or “friend.”
The Hebrew says “by the hand of Moses.” This was probably all or part of Deuteronomy.
Ahikam means “my brother has stood up.” Abdon means “servant.” Second Kings 22:12 calls him Achbor. Asaiah means “Yahweh has made.”
Huldah means “weasel” or “mole.” The meaning of Tokhath is uncertain. Second Kings 22:14 calls him Tikvah and calls Hasrah “Harhas.” The Second District was a newer part of Jerusalem.
The Hebrew word for “anger” here is a strong word for rage.
Josiah died in battle (35:23-24). But he died before the disaster came on Jerusalem, and he was buried in his own tomb.
The word for agreement is covenant.

verses.text: Josiah held a Passover for Yahweh in Jerusalem. On the fourteenth day of the first month (in March–April) the Passover lambs were killed.{a}
He gave the priests their duties and cheered them on as they served in Yahweh’s temple.

The Levites taught all Israel and were set apart for Yahweh. Josiah told them, “Place the holy ark in the temple built by Solomon, David’s son, who was king of Israel. Your shoulders are free of that load from now on. So serve Yahweh your God, and serve Israel, his people.{b}
Get ready to serve by your family groups and work teams. Follow what David, king of Israel, wrote down, and what his son Solomon wrote.
Take your places in the holy area. Let a group of Levites stand ready to help each family group of the ordinary people, your relatives.
Kill the Passover lambs. Make yourselves holy. Get everything ready for your relatives, so they can do what Yahweh told them through Moses.”
For the ordinary people who came, Josiah gave thirty thousand lambs and young goats for Passover offerings. He also gave three thousand bulls. All of these came from the king’s own herds and flocks.

His officials gave freely, too, to the people, the priests, and the Levites. God’s temple had three chief officers: Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel. For the priests’ Passover they supplied 2,600 lambs and goats and 300 bulls.{c}

The Levite leaders also gave gifts. Conaniah and his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel joined with Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad. Together they gave 5,000 lambs and goats and 500 bulls for the Levites’ Passover offerings.{d}
When all was ready, the priests stood in their places. The Levites lined up by their teams, following the king’s command.
Next came the killing of the Passover animals. The Levites skinned them, and the priests took the blood from them and sprinkled it.

The Levites set aside the parts for burnt offerings to give to each family group of the people. That way the people could offer them to Yahweh, as the book of Moses says. They did the same with the bulls.
Following the rules, they roasted the Passover animals over the fire. They cooked the other holy offerings in pots, kettles, and pans, and hurried to serve them to all the people.{e}

Once that was done, the Levites made a meal ready for their own group and for the priests. The priests, Aaron’s descendants, were busy until dark offering the burnt offerings and the fat. That is why the Levites cooked for both groups.

The singers, Asaph’s descendants, stayed at their posts, as David had ordered, along with Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, the king’s seer. The gatekeepers stayed at each gate. None of them had to leave their work, because their fellow Levites prepared their food.{f}
So on that one day, all the work for Yahweh’s service was done. The Passover was kept, and burnt offerings were made on Yahweh’s altar, just as King Josiah had commanded.
Every Israelite present celebrated the Passover then. For seven days after it they also held the Festival of Bread Without Yeast.

Israel had not seen a Passover like this one since the days of the prophet Samuel. None of Israel’s kings had ever held a Passover to match what Josiah held with the priests, the Levites, all of Judah and Israel who came, and the people of Jerusalem.{g}
It happened in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign.{h}
Some time after Josiah had set the temple in order, Neco, Egypt’s king, marched north to fight at Carchemish beside the Euphrates River. Josiah led his army out to stop him.{i}

Neco sent messengers with this word: “King of Judah, this is no quarrel of yours. I am not here to fight you today. I am at war with another kingdom. God wants me to move quickly. He is with me. Stop opposing God, or he will destroy you.”
Josiah would not turn back, though. He put on a disguise so he could go into battle. He did not listen to what Neco said, even though it came from God. He went to fight on the plain at Megiddo.{j}
Enemy archers hit King Josiah with arrows. “Get me out of here,” he told his servants. “I am badly hurt.”

His servants lifted the wounded king from his chariot into a second one that belonged to him. On the way to Jerusalem he died. They laid him in the family tombs where his ancestors lay. Across Judah and in Jerusalem, everyone grieved over Josiah’s death.{k}

Jeremiah wrote sad songs for Josiah. Even now, singers, both men and women, still name Josiah when they sing songs of mourning. Singing them became a custom in Israel. You can find them in the book called the Laments.{l}
The rest of what Josiah did, and the faithful deeds he did in keeping Yahweh’s Law,
everything from beginning to end, is written down in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.

notes.text: The first month was Nisan, also called Abib. Second Kings 23:21-23 tells about this Passover in only three verses.
The ark seems to have been taken out of the temple, maybe under Manasseh or Amon. We are not told why.
Jehiel means “God lives.” The Hebrew says “small cattle,” meaning sheep and goats.
Nethanel means “God has given.” Hashabiah means “Yahweh has counted.” Jeiel may mean “God has treasured.” See 31:12-15.
The Hebrew word means “cooked.” See Exodus 12:8-9 and Deuteronomy 16:7.
Asaph means “he has gathered.” Heman means “faithful.” Jeduthun may mean “praising.”
Second Kings 23:22 says “since the days of the judges.”
This was about 622 BC, the same year the book was found (34:8).
Neco ruled Egypt about 610-595 BC. Carchemish was a city on the Euphrates in northern Syria. In 609 BC Neco went to help the last king of Assyria against Babylon (2 Kings 23:29).
Megiddo was a city that guarded the pass into the Jezreel plain.
Second Kings 23:29-30 says he died at Megiddo and was carried dead to Jerusalem.
Jeremiah may mean “Yahweh lifts up.” These laments are not the book of Lamentations.

verses.text: Josiah’s son Jehoahaz was picked by the people of the land. They crowned him in Jerusalem to rule in his father’s place.{a}
Joahaz had reached twenty-three when the crown came to him. His reign in Jerusalem lasted just three months.{b}
Egypt’s king took the throne away from him in Jerusalem. He made the land pay about 3 3/4 tons of silver and about 75 pounds of gold.{c}
Then Egypt’s king put Eliakim, Joahaz’s brother, on the throne over Judah and Jerusalem. He gave Eliakim the new name Jehoiakim. Neco took Joahaz away to Egypt.{d}
Jehoiakim was twenty-five when he became king. He reigned eleven years from Jerusalem. He did evil in the sight of Yahweh his God.{e}
Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, attacked him. He put him in bronze chains to haul him away to Babylon.{f}
Nebuchadnezzar carried off some of the things from Yahweh’s temple too. He put them in his own temple in Babylon.
The book of the kings of Israel and Judah has the rest of Jehoiakim’s story, telling of the disgusting things he did and the evil that was in him. His son Jehoiachin followed him as king.{g}
At the age of eight Jehoiachin became king. Three months and ten days was all he reigned in Jerusalem. He too did evil in Yahweh’s eyes.{h}

When spring came, King Nebuchadnezzar had him carried off to Babylon. Valuable objects from Yahweh’s temple were taken there with him. Nebuchadnezzar made Jehoiachin’s relative Zedekiah king over Judah and Jerusalem.{i}
Zedekiah was twenty-one when he started his reign. He ruled from Jerusalem for eleven years.{j}
He did evil in the eyes of Yahweh his God. The prophet Jeremiah brought him messages from Yahweh, but Zedekiah refused to humble himself.
Nebuchadnezzar had made him swear in God’s name to be loyal. Even so, Zedekiah turned against him. He became stubborn and made his heart hard. He refused to come back to Israel’s God, Yahweh.

The priests’ leaders grew worse and worse in their unfaithfulness, and so did the people. They copied every disgusting practice of the nations. They made Yahweh’s temple unclean, the temple he had made holy in Jerusalem.
Yahweh, the God of their ancestors, felt pity for his people and for the place where he lived. So again and again he sent his messengers to warn them.
But they made fun of God’s messengers. They hated what he said and laughed at his prophets. At last Yahweh’s anger rose against his people, and nothing could heal them.

So Yahweh brought the king of the Chaldeans against them. That king killed their young men with the sword, right in the holy temple. He showed no pity to anyone, not to young men or young women, not to the old or the gray-haired. God gave every one of them into that king’s power.{k}
Every object in God’s temple, whether large or small, was carried to Babylon. So were the treasures of Yahweh’s temple, and the riches of the king and his officials.
God’s temple was burned, and Jerusalem’s wall was broken down. Every palace went up in flames, and everything of value was ruined.{l}
The people who lived through the killing he took away to Babylon. They became slaves to him and to his sons until Persia’s kingdom came to power.{m}
In this way the message Yahweh gave through Jeremiah came true. The land finally had its Sabbath rests. All the time it lay empty, it rested, until seventy years were complete.{n}

During Cyrus’s first year as Persia’s king, Yahweh acted to make the message he gave through Jeremiah come true. He moved the heart of Cyrus to send an announcement through his whole kingdom, both spoken and written. It said:{o}

“Cyrus, king of Persia, declares: Yahweh, the God of heaven, has put every kingdom on earth into my hands. He has chosen me to build him a temple in Jerusalem, in the land of Judah. Whoever among you belongs to his people may go there. May Yahweh your God be with you!”{p}

notes.text: Jehoahaz means “Yahweh has taken hold.” He was also called Shallum (1 Chronicles 3:15; Jeremiah 22:11). Verses 1-4 are much like 2 Kings 23:30-35. This was about 609 BC.
Joahaz is a shorter form of Jehoahaz. The Septuagint adds that his mother was Hamutal from Libnah, as in 2 Kings 23:31.
The Hebrew says “100 talents of silver and a talent of gold.” A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).
Eliakim means “God raises up.” Jehoiakim means “Yahweh raises up.” Second Kings 23:34 says Joahaz died in Egypt.
See 2 Kings 23:36-24:6. He ruled about 609-598 BC.
Nebuchadnezzar means “Nabu, protect the heir.” He was king of Babylon about 605-562 BC. Second Kings 24:6 does not say Jehoiakim was taken to Babylon (see Daniel 1:1-2).
Jehoiachin means “Yahweh makes firm.” He was also called Jeconiah and Coniah.
Second Kings 24:8 says “eighteen,” which fits the fact that he had wives (2 Kings 24:15). “Eight” here may be a copying mistake. This was in 597 BC.
Zedekiah means “Yahweh is right.” His first name was Mattaniah. The Hebrew says “brother,” but 2 Kings 24:17 calls him Jehoiachin’s uncle. “In the spring” is literally “at the turn of the year.”
See 2 Kings 24:18-25:21 and Jeremiah 52. Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC.
The Chaldeans were the people of southern Babylonia who ruled the Babylonian empire.
Second Kings 25:8-9 says this happened on the seventh day of the fifth month (in July–August). Jeremiah 52:12 says the tenth day.
Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC.
See Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10 and Leviticus 26:34-35, 43.
Cyrus was king of Persia about 559-530 BC. His first year over Babylon was 538 BC. Verses 22-23 are repeated at the start of Ezra (Ezra 1:1-3).
In the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles is usually the last book. So the Hebrew Bible ends with the call to “go up.” The Hebrew says “let him go up.”
